utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case, please, Mr. Court Deputy.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-01-48-T, the Prosecutor versus Sefer Halilovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. Good morning, Witness. Did you have a good rest yesterday?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We'll try to let you go back to spend your Easter at home. Yes, Ms. Chana.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: May it please Your Honours. If you'd give me a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honours. If you would give me a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes. Good morning, Mr. Hodzic.

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yesterday before the break, we were talking about the offensive which was supposed to have begun from Bugojno to Mostar and that was on the 13th of September. Now, did this offensive begin on that day?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not the entire area. Just one part of that area, in the direction of Crni Vrh, and probably somewhere from Bugojno. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And why was that?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we got back to Jablanica on the 12th, we realised that for the central, southern part of the front, things had not been prepared yet. And the telephone lines were not there, and so it was not possible to do anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Now, where did you go next on -- on the 13th of September?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 13th of September in the morning, I went to see Mr. Sefer Halilovic at Zuka's flat where he was staying and then we set out to Dobro Polje. Actually, we went to Voljevac and Dobro Polje. We were expecting some fighting because we heard shelling. Jablanica was being shelled.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And where did you go after that? Who did you see?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we got there, to the area of Dobro Polje where the fighters of the Prozor Battalion were, they were all resting basically and they should have been at the front line. Sefer -- and there was a fighter there who had a sense of humour, and we laughed a lot with him the day before. And he said, "Why are you lying around? Why aren't you fighting?" And he said, "Well, I'm awaiting orders." And then we found out that the Prozor Battalion did not go anywhere that morning, although it had been their task.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And why was it that they did not go into action that morning?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Enver Buza, the commander of the battalion, came rather fast, and he said, "Somebody is pulling somebody's leg here because I only got the fuel this morning at 4.00 a.m. and I had 2 litres of petrol before and I couldn't go into action because I didn't have any fuel." So he could not have his ambulances with him in case there were any wounded.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And how did Sefer Halilovic react to this news about the Prozor Independent Battalion not going into action?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he was very surprised, and he said -- well, he didn't want Buza's fighters to hear and he said, "Who made him a commander of the battalion anyway?"

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Did he say anything else?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think -- I think that -- he said that there were similar occasions in the past where three or four times similar situations arose. And I mean, he did not cause any unpleasantness in front of the fighters, but he said, "Let's go in the direction of Voljevac," and he asked him to come along. And then Braco Fazlic came along, who was the deputy or the Chief of Staff of the commander of the 6th Corps. And I asked him, "Well, who put Buza there?" And he said, "I did. He's a good man."

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: But what was Sefer Halilovic's demeanour towards Enver Buza?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, he did not cause any problems in front of the men, but he said to him to come down to Voljevac, the village that we were going to.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And was there any other meeting with Enver Buza that you heard and Sefer Halilovic?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was when we got to Voljevac.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And what happened then?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We got there first, before they did, and there was Bilajac there. So it was a private home owned by some man, and we got to that house and Bilajac, Suljevic, and Karic were there and Enver Zejnilagic. And we were later joined by Buza and Braco Fazlic.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes. And what were they discussing?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Sefer told him that he did not carry out his task and that he had to go into operation the day after and that Suljevic was to accompany him.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Why did he want to send Suljevic with him?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I suppose he didn't really trust him to go -- to go into operation. I suppose.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: All right. And then what did you do after that?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We spent almost a whole day there. We were following combat operations. We went to the liaison centre in the basement, all of us, and fighting was underway. And our fighters took Gvozd. That was the name. And everything looked great in the beginning, but later on in the afternoon we heard the news that one of the most famous farmers -- fighters, other, of Neretvica fell. So I went out and I was interviewing someone. But at any rate, we were there. We were following combat operations and then we went back.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Did you ever hear anything about what happened during this combat in Uzdol?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was prior to the fighting in Uzdol. It was before they went to Uzdol.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: No, but did you ever discover any -- any crimes, if they had been committed, in Uzdol?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On that day, there could have been no crimes, because nobody left their bases. It happened the day after.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes. And what happened the day after?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the day after, this real fighting was supposed to start in the real area, in the intended area, the area that we had organised it all for in order to go in the direction of Mostar. And it was Sefer's plan to go in the -- towards the south, in the direction of Mostar, and not Prozor. And I myself wished to be there as well and to follow what was going on. But we heard nothing in the morning, to the south, in the direction of Mostar. There was no fighting there. And at around 10.00, slightly after 10.00 perhaps, I went to Zuka's flat and I visited Sefer Halilovic, and he was sitting there playing with the son, and his escorts were there and I said, "Sefer, there's nothing going on down there," because I was more to the south. My accommodation was is there, in Grabovica. And I said, "Well look, nothing seems to be going on. And then -- but there is fighting in Prozor." We could hear explosions. And he made a phone call and he said, "Yes, it's true. Nothing is going down there. Let's go in the direction of Prozor."

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And did you go?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And we set out at around 1.00 p.m. We arrived at Dobro Polje, where the base was, the base of the Prozor Battalion. It was a kind of shack, in fact. And there was a small house where you could have two or three people inside and it was the liaison centre. I don't know how Sefer found out about it, but I found out, I was told -- I mean, I wasn't there when Sefer was talking to them, but I did hear that fighters of the Prozor Battalion entered Uzdol early and they found the Ustashas asleep and they - that's what they said - and they killed quite a few of them. And -- but then that the HVO counterattack, they started shelling, and then they withdrew.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And the soldiers were telling Sefer this, was it?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To me. That's what I heard. And I don't know what Sefer heard. I suppose he must have heard it as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: But he was there at the time.

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was. But I did not witness his conversation with them. I assume that he would have heard it as well. Because I went straight into the shack that I mentioned before. I didn't go to the liaison centre. And that's what I was told. And then I came by the liaison centre and they were standing at the door and they said, "Well, yes, everything is okay but the soldiers are withdrawing." And Sefer was there with his escorts. And there were a couple of women there, some elderly people and he was talking to them. And we got in the car straight away and went in -- and went in the direction of Voljevac. But the impression was that it was a fight which was okay, a battle which was okay, but they had to withdraw. And there was no mention of anything else.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: But there was mention that people had been killed.

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that they found them asleep in their pyjamas. And they said their fights were found asleep at some school. They surprised them in their sleep. That was the story.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And did you write a report about this on that day?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not. I did not write any reports on that day.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Did you watch CNN on that day?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We went down to Voljevac and then we went back to Mostar, and -- I can't really remember. No, it couldn't have been on that day, because we went straight to Donja Jablanica in the evening, and I myself went to Dreznica, and there was indeed fighting when we came back. I did not find or see anyone from the Prozorski Battalion, Sefer or Buza or anything else. We got back and I didn't go back there. I went to Dreznica and I stayed there another day. And then I got back. And then I visited a cousin of mine and she mentioned that perhaps she saw on the CNN or on some other TV station that there was some crime committed in Uzdol and that some civilians had been killed. And I thought that it was about these soldiers who were asleep and killed in their sleep, in their pyjamas. But whilst I was there, we saw excerpts from that report on some TV station. I can't remember which one. And that was the time when I actually found out that something had happened there. But I was not at all sure. I mean, even until the end of the war, we were not sure that any crimes had been committed in Uzdol, whether it was some sort of orchestrated operation that they had put dead Bosniaks there, that apparently there was snow seen there but there was really no snow. And for years after the war there were some doubts in our minds as to whether any crimes had actually been committed there, and a great deal has been written about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: But at that day on the 14th, when you discovered at this centre that people had been killed, what time was that? And how long were you with Sefer on that particular day? When did you -- if you did indeed part company?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stayed with Sefer throughout that period. We went to Voljevac and then we went in the direction of either Gornji or Donji Vakuf, I can't remember. And then we went back through Dobro Polje to Jablanica. And then we went to Donje Jablanica straightaway, where Zuka's base was and we separated. And I went in the direction of Dreznica with Celo's fighters. We walked through the night basically. And they were fighting -- there were battles there. And that was it.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: So when -- when you heard about this, you -- you did not go back to where the -- the combat activity was of the Prozor Independent Battalion to find out what happened.

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, we didn't. And it wasn't possible anyway, because we had already been told that the Prozor Battalion had withdrawn, that they were no longer at Uzdol, that they were withdrawing. I really don't know exactly where that place Uzdol is.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And how -- how many days after did you actually see this on the CNN or hear about it? When you -- you said your cousin told you that it was on the CNN.

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I had to kind of put it all together in my mind, all this information. Because we went away from Voljevac and we went through Jablanica and Donja Jablanica and then I went to Dreznica and I spent there one night and another day until the evening, and then in the evening I went back to Donja Jablanica. So it might have been on the 16th, the 17th, or the 18th. That was the period roughly. One of those days, but I'm not sure which one.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Then what did you do after that?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After what?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: The next day, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the next day, I was following the fighting in the direction of Mostar at a place called Dreznica. There was a blockade there. And the blockade was lifted because some surrounding areas had been liberated and I went to the centre and I filmed a little bit and I sent in a very short report from Dreznica.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Did you go to Grabovica at any time?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went through Grabovica that evening. When I left Zuka's base to go to Grabovica, I had to go through Grabovica, and I remember this. It was at night and we were standing outside and I remember -- well, I don't really know who else was there, whether it was in front of Adnan's base or Celo's base. I've forgotten. But at any rate, I do remember I saw Caco there. And I talked to him a little bit, and he had forgotten who I was. He said, "You have to remind me. I'm sorry, I don't remember you." And then we made small talk and then three or four of Celo's fighters came by - Malco Rovcanin and two people and a guide, whose name was Joja - and we spent four hours going to Dreznica on foot across these hills and mountains, and we got there at about 1.00 a.m.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Was Sefer Halilovic with you at this time?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He stayed in Donja Jablanica.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Did you ever go back to the village of Grabovica with Sefer Halilovic a few days later?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recollect the date exactly. I suppose it must have been the 18th of November -- no.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The speaker corrects himself.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] September. When fighting continued in the south and -- we went to an artillery position. And from there Sefer tried to get in touch with Zuka, who was the commander of this entire front line, and his deputy, Nihad, and I don't really know where Nihad was. But they never managed to get in touch with them. Now, I seem to have forgotten something here. But I suppose, I assume, I'm not at all sure -- but what I'm going to tell you now actually happened. We went through Grabovica. We went by an iron bridge, and then we went to a house, and Caco was there. I do remember Caco. There were quite a few fighters there. And later on they started playing ball. I suppose they finished their game, but that was probably on that day. I don't remember us going to Grabovica ever again except on the 19th. And then there is a picture in my mind of fighters diving into the Neretva and -- they were fishing, basically, and every time they came back up, they had a fish. And Caco was there and he was laughing, and I tried to take a photo of him, but all the people around gave me a nasty look. And Rovcanin then took my camera and he wanted to take his picture and then they gave him a nasty look as well, and so he didn't dare either. And then I went to Jablanica, Donja Jablanica, and that's what I remember, my time with Sefer in Grabovica until the next day.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes. I'm going to ask you to hear something.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is the -- we will listen to this recording through Sanction, Your Honour. It is -- 65 ter is 177, T0000585.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be MFI291.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Can you tell us what that was, please, Mr. Hodzic.

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a recording of one of my extended talks with a number of fighters and commanders: Celo, Adnan, his -- or Celo's and Caco's fighters who a couple of days before had been in combat operations. And even some of them came back from Dreznica with me, some of Celo's people, because I think six of his people were wounded there. And in the end, there was this conversation. We were all enthusiastic. And if you could have the entire tape, you could hear the atmosphere basically. And then when we found out that Medvjed had been freed and five times more than that, as Zuka had said. So we were having this rather euphoric conversation and things dampened down a little bit when we finally reached Sefer, because we had already been talking about it for an hour. And then as you can see, at the very end I asked Mr. Halilovic to say a few words as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: So that was Mr. Halilovic, was it, that you were talking to?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And do you remember the date?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. The 19th of September, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And you say that: "So the Sarajevans are defending Herzegovina and the Chief of Staff is here of the Supreme Command, which I know this very well. He organised it, conceived it, and so on and so forth." Now, can you tell me when this was -- Halilovic is talking about the troops from Sarajevo. Who was he referring to?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think fighters from the Sarajevo units which got there and which in a way, a month before, became famous in stopping the Serb offensive at Igman. It was the same units. And they even managed to recapture some of the positions there. The name of one of the places was Tresnjevo Brdo.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Now, just to be quite clear about this, Mr. Hodzic, was this interview after the crimes in Grabovica and Uzdol?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It is the 19th.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And was anything mentioned at the time about what had happened in Grabovica?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was thinking in terms of a story, Sarajevans defending Herzegovina. And when I talked to Sefer about Grabovica, we talked about that. And then I went through the story that we discussed yesterday. So there was no other story there.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours. I'm just looking at my question, and I had said: "Was anything mentioned at the time about what happened in Grabovica?" I meant and Uzdol as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: So would you answer -- would your answer be the same for Grabovica and Uzdol?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: No?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, nothing there. We -- we didn't make any reference to Uzdol or Grabovica at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Ms. Chana, do you have the English transcript for that recording?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The transcript should be in evidence. Let me -- excuse me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. We have it.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Now, there is another document I wish to show you. This is your diary, Mr. Hodzic, and its 65 ter number is 126 -- I'm sorry. Can I take that back. It's 106. It's 01057700.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be MFI292.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Mr. Hodzic, I'm just going to show you a small portion from your diary. It will come up on your screen in a minute. And it's dated "Jablanica 1st October 1993." Is it on your screen now, Mr. Hodzic?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: It's not on your screen?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: If you could please scroll down to 01057848 to 01057849. It's the last portion of the diary, and the entry is on 1st October 1993.

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Is that your diary, Mr. Hodzic, that you see before you?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Yes. Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And it starts with: "Amela came and told Sefer while we were in Zuka's camp, 'One of the soldiers wants to squeeze your hand.'" And then it goes on to say: "Sefer told her to let him in. He had a badge with Sefer's face pinned on his chest and he said his name was Nasko Softic." I would like to ask you in respect of the badge, you saw that badge of Sefer's face pinned onto the soldier's chest.

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Had you seen such badges before, or was that the first time you saw such a badge?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that was the first time. Perhaps I'd seen such badges before, but that's what I remember and that's what I wrote down.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Had you heard that badges -- that some soldiers were bearing badges with Sefer Halilovic's face on it? Picture on it. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible that I had -- or I may not have. It didn't mean much to me. I really can't say. I think I laid eyes on that badge for the first time then and perhaps I never saw it again. But I really can't say. I may have heard before, and I may have not, but that's when I saw it.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Why would it be, Mr. Hodzic, that soldiers would be wearing badges?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: I see counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, my friend does see counsel objecting and I don't want any speculative questions to be asked, Your Honour, so I object to that one. In particular, the witness has made it clear that he saw this particular soldier on the -- I think the date in the diary is specified as being the 1st of October, 1993. And that's the only occasion he recalls doing it. Now, for my friend to say "why would soldiers wear such a badge" is -- well, it's speculative and I object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. You may ask "that particular soldier."

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Why do you think that particular soldier who came into Zuka's base was wearing a badge with Sefer's picture on it?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't say. Like many other fighters, he probably liked Sefer. There were many mothers at the time who named their son after Sefer, although I had not been aware of the name in Bosnia prior to that time. But that's only my interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And what -- very briefly, what were the circumstances of the -- what was the purport of the conversation between the soldier and Sefer?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can see it right here. I'll read it out for you. He says his name is Nasko Softic from Bijelo Polje. He says he's been wearing the badge from day one, since it first appeared. He said, "I've been listening to the radio and Sefko Hodzic's reports." And then it goes on. He said he was an employee of the Ministry of the Interior. They listened to my reports over the radio. And there were 105 of them volunteering to go to Herzegovina and to fight, but they were employees of the Ministry of the Interior and they were forbidden -- they were banned from going and threatened to be fired in case they went to Herzegovina. 105 of them still decided to go, even at the risk of losing their jobs. They went to see their boss and they said, "We are here to say goodbye because we want to go down and join the fray, join the fighting." So they did eventually. It was later on that I found out that the MUP, the Ministry of the Interior, had filed criminal complaints against those people. Actually, he was the one I met and he told me that they had fired him.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Hodzic, I want to ask you a final question in respect of this part of the evidence. This is much later on now. Did you hear of Operation Trebevic?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And after that operation, did you have occasion to meet Mr. Sefer Halilovic?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 28th of July or possibly August [as interpreted], I got a call from the chief of the public security station in Sarajevo, Munir Alibabic, in a threatening tone of voice. And this is what he told me: "Today at 11.00 you should go and speak to Enver Mujezinovic, chief of the SDB. Bring all your tapes, all your footage, your diary, everything you have so we don't come looking for you." Why was it that he said that? He said, "You spoke well of people who had committed crimes over there." And I said, "Those were no criminals. Those were our fighters." He threatened me again and said, "Be there at 11.00." So I gathered all my tapes and everything that I later handed over to you. I had no more tapes at one point, so I had to I raise the old ones to record reports on new battles. I gathered all my stuff and there I was 11.00 sharp outside the SDB building. That very moment Sefer came down the street and entered the same building by some coincidence. We came in together. I asked him, "Sefer, are you in trouble too?" And he said, "Indeed I am. They are trying to frame me," something along these lines, something to the effect that he was behind those people there, Caco, Celo. Caco had already been killed by this time. And he told them, "I created a state for you. I created an army. And now you may as well arrest me if you like."

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Hodzic, there's one clarification. The transcript has said you said "28th of July or possibly August." That can't be -- that cannot be the correct date.

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. October.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I may have mixed them up. It was 22 or 23 days following the Trebevic operation.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes. Well, that was in October, so if that -- that date --

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: October, yes. The 27th, possibly the 28th of October, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes. Now, one final document. And this would be MFI --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Sorry, could I just intervene for one second? I think there's -- I'm sorry. Pardon me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I apologise for interrupting. We think there's a translation issue there which we'd just like to have clarified. On page 17 at line 16, the translation says: "I may have mixed them up. It was 22 or 23 days following the Trebevic operation." My instructions from the Bosnian speaker here is that the witness said two or three days, not 22 or 23. Could we just ask for a translator's clarification of that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, maybe Ms. Chana could re-ask this question to this witness, because that's important.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Mr. Hodzic, could you please clarify this for us. Was it 22 or 23 days or was it 2 or 3 days following the Operation Trebevic?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two or three days after, after the operation commenced. The 27th or possibly 28th of October, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hodzic. The next document is MFI281. This, Mr. Hodzic, is a book written by Sefer Halilovic, and there's a chapter there which relates to events. Firstly, have you read Mr. Halilovic's book "Cunning Strategy"?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was there when the book was published. There was a ceremony attended by the present-day president of the Republic of Croatia, Stipe Mesic, and one of the people that published the book. That's when I purchased the book and I read it over the following two days.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And do you see that particular chapter before you on the screen now?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. "The Truth about Uzdol," that's what I can see.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And you're familiar with the events that Mr. Halilovic writes about in this particular chapter? You've read it?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Would you say that this is an accurate rendition of the events as you also witnessed them?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's interesting to know that there are quite a number of things that I didn't witness myself, certain documents that I never obtained, especially in relation to the briefing at Zenica. These decisions -- and he spends a lot of time speaking about what the commander spoke about among themselves at meetings that I never attended. When I read this, I saw two or three areas, in terms of dates, and that's all I can say about it. I've got nothing else to say. This is Sefer's account, and there is nothing I can add to it.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And what -- what do you mean "in terms of dates"?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure. If I were to go through this again, I think he got the date wrong when the offensive commenced. He said the 13th -- or rather, he said the 12th, and to the best of my recollection, it was the 13th in actual fact. The time we went out together, I think he said the 2nd of October, and I believe it may have been on the 31st of August. And then we got to Jablanica. These are not technical issues really, nothing essential. He just got a few dates wrong. That's all.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Now, again, I'll seek a clarification on the date. The record reflects that you said 2nd of October. You probably meant 2nd of September.

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. Yes, precisely, 2nd of September. I think that's what it says, if we were to go through this again. But I do believe there were a handful of errors there. That's what I noticed.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Hodzic.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Your Honour, that would be my examination-in-chief. As promised to you, tops 40 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Any cross, Mr. Morrissey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, yes, there is, Your Honour. But I just want to raise one matter before we commence, and that is in terms of the -- of the -- the book of Mr. Halilovic. Now, it is a matter we've got to raise later on, but it's one of those matters that ought to be canvassed now because sometimes if counsel cross-examine on a document, that becomes a basis in some cases for it to be tendered -- for it to be admitted into the evidence. And I just want to know where I stand, effectively, in regard to that, because at the moment what I'll be submitting at the end, I make it quite clear, there's been no sufficient basis for that document to be tendered through this witness, no more than with the previous witness. But I don't want to then cross-examine the witness on it and place everyone in the position where they'd say, "Well, now there's a new reason to tender it through this witness," because I've cross-examined on it. So I just seek that the Prosecutor clarify that now, because I need to know what the consequences are for me cross-examining on that document before I start. And I want to know whether the Prosecutor is intending still to attempt to put that document into evidence through Mr. Hodzic based on what he's now said. I would seek that clarification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Chana.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We are certainly asking to tender all the exhibits that were listed through this witness. But I can ask now for all my exhibits to be tendered into evidence, including Mr. Halilovic's book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I -- I'm in a position to respond now. It may be appropriate to give the witness a break then at this point before I commence cross-examination. I certainly can respond to my learned friend's motion to tender these documents now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, maybe we could deal with the document at a later stage, as we did usually. We don't have time. Maybe we could have the written decisions at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: And I don't think any cross-examination will add any weight for consideration of this Bench to have it admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I believe that everybody is free -- since it's a publicly available document, everybody is free to comment on the document, to offer their own views concerning of that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, I'm -- yes, I -- thank you for that indication. And I'm ready to proceed to -- to cross-examine Mr. Hodzic now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Hodzic. Could I just ask you firstly about some matters that arise before the combat down in -- in -- in Herzegovina. You became aware that Sefer Halilovic was replaced as the leader of the Bosnian Armed Forces on the 8th of June, 1993 by Rasim Delic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. And you became aware that from that time on Sefer Halilovic performed the function of Chief of Staff of the Bosnian army, although Rasim Delic was the commander of the staff of the Bosnian army; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. And did you become aware that there was - I won't go into the details of, this but just the timing factor - that on the 2nd of July, perhaps the night of the 2nd and the early morning of the 3rd of July, there was some sort of armed confrontation between members of the 9th and 10th Brigade on the one hand, and members of the MUP and certain civil -- certain military security officers on the other hand? Did you become aware that -- in broad terms that such a confrontation did take place on that date?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I became aware of that. But that was much later, because I wasn't in Sarajevo at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. And I'm certainly not going to ask you to -- to comment on that -- on the substance of that confrontation. It's just the date that I'm really interested in now. Okay. So that happened on the 2nd. Now, on the 7th of July -- I'm sorry, I'll just -- I'll just wait a moment. Okay. Now, on the -- were you aware that five days after that armed conflict -- that armed conflict took place that you heard about, that Sefer Halilovic's wife and his brother-in-law were blown up while standing on the balcony of Sefer Halilovic's flat? In other words, on the 7th of July, that Sefer Halilovic's wife was killed by an explosion.

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was two or three days later that I found out about it. I was at Igman at the time, and that's what I was told. Someone from the command told me what had occurred, and they said that they would be expressing their condolences in due course.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Sorry. Sorry, Counsel. I'm not sure that we got a year. 7th of July of what year?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I apologise for that. The transcript doesn't reveal what year.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Was that on the 7th of July -- the 7th of July, 1993?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I read in Sefer's book, and I heard later that that's indeed what it was, but I was at Igman when I heard that Sefer's wife had been killed. Apparently that was true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. And did you hear that as well as Sefer's wife being killed that Sefer's brother-in-law, a dark-haired man dressed in a military uniform at the time, was also killed by the same explosion on the same balcony?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's what I read in the book.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And -- very well. And did the -- did the death of Sefer's wife cause some interest in the local press at the time when it happened?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was outside Sarajevo between the 24th of June and the 26th of July. No newspapers there, only Oslobodjenje, which was actually published in Sarajevo, but nothing from outside. There was combat going on, and I was all over the hills at the time. I have no idea what the media said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Sorry, well, you've -- I think you've answered my questions. You didn't come back into Sarajevo until after the 26th of July; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was combat going on at Igman, and I was sending my reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. Well, look, in that event, I won't proceed to ask you any questions about that phase. All right. Just to move on now. You had come to know Sefer Halilovic over the course of the war, commencing in 1992, and you'd had the opportunity to observe him as the leader of the army quite closely in that time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true. I met him on the 28th of May, five [Realtime transcript read in error: "1995"] days after he was appointed. Ever since -- he was fair to all journalists, and the same applies to me. He was reluctant about giving interviews, but we had satisfactory cooperation on the whole.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. I'm sorry. The transcript has revealed that you said you met him on 28 May 1995. I wonder if that may just be an error, either in translation or --

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 1992. That was five days after he was appointed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Thank you. We just have to correct these -- these as they arise, Mr. Hodzic, but thank you for that. Okay. Well, and in that time, your observation of Sefer Halilovic was that he was an officer who was dedicated to a unified and multi-ethnic Bosnia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. And the same applies to all Bosnian patriots at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. And indeed it was apparent to you that during the time when Sefer Halilovic was in control of the army, during the time when he was the head man of the army, before the 8th of June, that he made it quite clear at all times that the army was to respect the multi-ethnic character of the Bosnian state; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was at the same time that the Presidency reached their own platform, and everything was headed in that direction, and Sefer very much held his own at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. I'm going to ask you some -- some more specific questions about what Sefer said on this topic down in Herzegovina, and I'm really just asking you some preliminary questions now about what he'd said at earlier times. Had you observed Sefer to introduce various rules into the army designed to bring the army, the Bosnian army, under the command-and-control system in an organised way?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I saw documents to that effect too, and I witnessed it myself, and I know that he was the one who established the command-and-control system and made the Bosnian army a soldierly organisation, to the extent that he could, because after all it was an army of volunteers by and large.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. And -- and in particular -- okay. Well, I'll come to some specific questions about his political position -- or sorry, his -- his goals when we get to the questions about Herzegovina. Now, after -- you indicated that you met Sefer in Konjic when you were attempting to resolve the situation with your -- your mother's travel. And you indicated at that time that he'd -- he'd indicated that he was going to Mostar as well. Now, at that time, did he tell you that he was going to coordinate the operation down in -- or coordinate combat actions, I should say? Did he tell you that he was going to coordinate combat actions in Herzegovina, and in particular did he use the word "koordinacija"?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, he did not use that word at the time. It was once we arrived - I didn't write this down - and it was only what I wrote down in my reports. Maybe he said "exercise control" or maybe something slightly different. But I'm quite sure he didn't actually use the term "coordination." Because later when ever on when I asked him on the record, "What's your role," he said "coordinator." But he had originally used a different expression, or that was my impression. And that's what I wrote down at the time: "Exercise control." But I don't have that in writing. I didn't actually record anything at the time the minute he said it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: No, that's okay. Could you just say for the benefit of the Court, if you can remember the precise word that he used at Konjic, are you able to say what that is? If you can't recall it, that's fine too.

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say specifically, but that's what I remember. He said he would be exercising control. He may have said something else, but that's what remained with me, the expression he used.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: That's okay. But you've indicated that in due course you clarified that on the record with him at -- in Herzegovina. And I just wonder, could you specify for the Tribunal when it was - if you can remember the date, that would help - but when it was that he placed this word "koordinacija" on the record.

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have it right here in my diary. I believe you have a copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was preparing that particular report, and I couldn't quite put my finger on the date. I had trouble defining the exact date. It was -- I was just turning the pages. There were still some blank pages to go. And it may be that actually what was published was something that happened later on in relation to what had been recorded in my diary. I believe it was prior to the commencement of operations. That's my impression, but I didn't actually write it down. It may have been on the 12th, but it was certainly just on the eve of the operation. That was when I interviewed him. I said, "There's an operation due to commence tomorrow." And I said, "What would you say about your own role, commander?" And he said, "Coordinator." And that's precisely what I wrote down at the time: "Sefer - coordinator," and you can see it right here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: All right. Do you -- because your diary is your own document, do you have a copy of that diary in front of you right now?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. Look, what I might do is come back to that question in the break and -- and give you the opportunity to -- to identify that. Thanks. Sorry. Okay. Thank you for that. Now, I did jump forward there and -- and I'd asked you some questions about what happened in Konjic. Now I want to go to -- directly to the -- what happened in Herzegovina. When you got down -- could I just indicate to you as well, Mr. Hodzic, I'm not going to -- I'm not going to go over every -- every question that you've been asked by the learned Prosecutor who -- who took you through these matters in a fairly complete sort of a way, so it's specific details I'll be going to. Now, when you got down to -- to Herzegovina, on that first night, as far as you know, Sefer stayed in Zuka's flat; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: When he was staying up in -- up in the -- the more northern area near to the Independent Prozor Battalion or the 45th Brigade or Operations Group Zapad, where was it his habit to stay when in that area?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We visited the commands of those units, but as far as I know, we never spent the night. We always went back.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: There's been some evidence in this court of Mr. Halilovic spending a night or more than one night actually at the -- at a facility called the ARK in Konjic. Does that jog your memory in any way?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's something else. That was from the 4th or the 5th. It was not the Prozor area. It was in the direction of Konjic. We spent a night there between the 4th and the 5th together with Delic, Cibo, Suljevic, Ranje [phoen]. We had dinner together and we stayed together for a long time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. I understand. And do you recall whether you met an individual named Mitke Perkic on that -- on the night of the 4th and the 5th in Konjic?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mitke Perkic used to be the commander of the 43rd Mountain Brigade from Konjic. And when we reached Konjic on the 4th, together with Delic -- well, not in the same car with Delic but perhaps within 10 minutes of one another, Mr. Delic and Mr. Halilovic and -- and the others held a meeting at the command with this guy Perkic and that command from Konjic. And I myself, as usual, was not present at the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: That was a military meeting, was it?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a military meeting, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, okay. Very well. Now, on the occasion when you arrived on the 1st of September, 1993 with Sefer, you indicated that he'd said to you words to the effect, "You do your job, and I'll do mine." What did you take him to be saying to you on that occasion? What did you understand that to be all about?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what it was supposed to mean, but at a later stage -- well, we had nice relations and perhaps it was meant like for me not to mind if I was not allowed to be present at those meetings. I mean, that was my assessment. I can't really say with any degree of certainty that that's what was meant. Perhaps that I was not there at the meetings. But I mean, it was the same in the past. Whenever there were battles going on, I never participated in meetings. And -- but that was certainly what he said. That was -- and I mean, he didn't interfere with my job and I, of course, couldn't have anything to do with his.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. And thank you. I was really asking -- really directing the question towards the question of his interfering with you. Did Sefer Halilovic ever interfere with the content of your reports? And in particular, did he do so in Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, no, no. He had no idea what I was writing about, where I was writing. I did say yesterday that I wrote my reports at the police station. They were the only ones who had a typewriter. And then I sent in my reports and he was nowhere in sight.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. I understand. Very well. Now, you also indicated yesterday when you were giving evidence that you had a discussion with Sefer. I can't remember if it was on the 1st of September or the 2nd. You can tell us that answer. But you had a discussion with him concerning the Owen-Stoltenberg Plan and what his opinion about that plan was. Could you give us a bit more detail about that discussion and in particular what Sefer's position was about the Owen-Stoltenberg Plan. Or perhaps to start with, maybe you could explain to the Tribunal very briefly as well what you understood the Owen-Stoltenberg Plan to be and then say what Sefer thought about it.

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to Stoltenberg's plan -- three months before I wrote this series of articles in 40 instalments. I studied the documents, all the materials telling about what was happening there. So I do know. I'm very familiar with this. It was a slightly modified plan of the proposal -- a joint proposal put forward by Milosevic and Tudjman that was presented in Geneva on the 14th of June, 1993 for Bosnia to be divided up into three parts - according to Milosevic, into three republics; and according to Tudjman, into three provinces. And the President Izetbegovic was there and he actually left, walked out of that meeting. And over the coming few days, he resisted it and then there were meetings in Zagreb and Owen was threatening both Izetbegovic and the others, and he managed to kind of break the other members of the Presidency and he managed to win over Fikret Abdic completely. And at a certain point President Izetbegovic also kind of relented under threat and accepted the division of Bosnia into three republics, with the proviso that the Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina approved it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, as of the time of the Neretva -- sorry, I won't use Neretva. Now, as at the time of the combat operations in Herzegovina -- well, perhaps I'll take a step back. Until the 27th of September, 1993, that Assembly of Bosnia had not yet approved that plan; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If -- if I did write about it -- I think until the 27th of September, I think -- no. No, no, no, no, not on the next day. No, it was later.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: So as -- just to be clear for the Tribunal -- the Tribunal has to have only a limited interest in this matter. But just to be clear, in -- at the time of the -- at the time the killings took place in Grabovica and Uzdol, the Assembly -- the Bosnian Assembly had not yet approved that Owen-Stoltenberg Plan to be adopted; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I think that it was for the Assembly on the 28th or the 29th of September. I think. There were quite a few conditions attached.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. Well, I'm just concerned with the timing now. And now I'll ask you some questions about this -- more about the substance of it. Very briefly, the Owen-Stoltenberg Plan involved the division of the State of Bosnia along the lines of local provinces or local cantons into the three republics or provinces that you've described; is that correct? And, in fact, it was a division along -- effectively along ethnic lines.

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mostly, yes, but not into provinces. Into republics. So Milosevic's original proposal, not Tudjman's original proposal, was approved. And that was the operational term, as it were. But along the ethnic lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: All right. Now, in the time before the Bosnian Assembly had to deal with the proposal by Owen and Stoltenberg, to which you've indicated Mr. Izetbegovic was leaning, what view did Sefer Halilovic express of that particular political solution when he spoke to you?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sefer Halilovic repeated that at least 10 times a day in different situations, and it was a burden for him, and he kept saying that Bosnia should not be divided up, that we could not allow for that, and that it had to be a single country.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. And after the Zenica meeting, which you didn't attend, did Sefer Halilovic express happiness that the army had resolved to continue to -- to fight for a unified Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's correct. When I met him at Konjic, I asked him - and that was on the 23rd of August, 1993 - I said, "What did you agree, Sefer, in relation to that plan?" And he said, "No way. No division of Bosnia," and he was very pleased. And so the war was going to go on until the country was freed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Now, when you got down to Herzegovina, you had a discussion with him, as you mentioned to my learned friend the Prosecutor yesterday. And what did he say about that topic when you talked about that with him in Herzegovina on the 1st or 2nd of -- of September?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was at Zuka's base. We stayed there until 2.00 or 3.00 a.m. and Selmo Cikotic came along with his group of people. And we discussed this at great length. And he talked about how he disagreed with President Izetbegovic on that point and Bosnia should not be divided. So that was the bottom line.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. And leaving aside Sefer Halilovic for a moment, were you aware that within Bosnia there was at that time a strong political debate between those who favoured the Izetbegovic solution of agreeing to some modified form of the Owen-Stoltenberg Plan on the one hand, and those on the other hand who rejected the Owen-Stoltenberg Plan altogether?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no, Izetbegovic agreed -- well, he was the one talking on our behalf and in principle he had agreed to this division, but he set quite a few conditions because he was against the idea of it being divided along ethnic lines. And he asked -- I mean, it is known because of the session of the National Assembly and there was a heated debate on that occasion. And one MP - I think his surname was Softic - he attacked and accused President Izetbegovic for going along with that proposal. He said that it would be the end of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and there were some other people as well. But the most outspoken opponent was Muhamed Filipovic, and he, too, was very much against this division. And Izetbegovic tried to do a balancing act there. He was against the division. He was not in favour of the division, as it was being suggested by Owen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. Well, thank you for that -- for that explanation. Now, just remaining on the 1st of September for a moment. I just want to ask you some questions about the village -- the visit that was paid to the village of Grabovica on that first day. Do you recall driving down to Grabovica with -- with Sefer Halilovic and Vehbija Karic and a number of others and stopping on the left bank of that village?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: All right. And you -- I think you indicated that there was -- before you spoke to the Igman Wolves, there was some discussion that took place with some of the local refugees who were living on the left bank. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the left side, yes, there were shacks where the builders lived, working on the power plant, and there were people who had been released from Dretelj and other camps of the HVO. There were some refugees, but the dominant group were the people who were released from camps, and they were worn out, et cetera, and we did talk to them and I took some pictures and they gathered round us and we spent some time with them, about half an hour, because we needed to press ahead. So we left.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And to the extent that you could hear what Sefer Halilovic was saying, what did Sefer Halilovic say to these people who gathered around?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't remember. I published it, and it's probably mentioned in one of the articles, and I recorded it and it was on the radio as well. But people were complaining to us. One of them said, for example, that for three days and three nights they didn't get any water. One actually said that he had to drink his own urine. And one said that they were being beaten up. And so it was a very heavy atmosphere. And they looked awful, these people. And he did give them some hope that -- he kept telling them that there was some hope for -- for them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. I just wanted the to ask you to exercise your memory and see if you can recall this. We've heard some evidence from -- actually from -- I can't say their names but from local people who were of Croat nationality and they said they took in some refugees into their homes. And I just want to ask you: Do you recall meeting any of the -- any of the local Croatian people on that occasion or, alternatively, any of the Muslim people who had been taken in by such Croats?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall that. I don't think so. No, no. We didn't go to any of those houses, because we were in a hurry. We were travelling fast from one place to another.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I see. So was this really just a gathering out in the open beside the road near to the Igman Wolves' huts?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in front of the huts. It was a big courtyard above the road between Konjic and Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Thank you for that. Now, on the 2nd of September -- well, perhaps I won't put on the 2nd of September. Do you recall -- do you recall seeing Mr. Cikotic at some stage while you were in Herzegovina in the -- in the first day or so that you arrived down there?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On -- on the 2nd or the 3rd, sometime around the 2nd and -- perhaps the first -- the first night or the second night. But at that initial stage. That's where I met him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. Look, I just wanted to clarify something that might give a flavour of what was happening down there. Did he tell you about a particular cannon that was taken from the museum down there and used?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether it was him exactly who said that to me, but I am familiar with the story. It was a Howitzer 115 millimetres from World War II and fighters got it out of a museum and -- and they nicknamed it Nana, and they kind of repaired it a little bit. And I think Cikotic told me -- if that was when it happened. But I do know that Nana had a facelift, basically. And -- if that's what you have in mind. So yeah. There was this rejuvenation effort.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I take it from what you observed artillery guns were in quite short supply for the Bosnian army down in Herzegovina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw one only, a 155 millimetres -- or maybe two. I don't know. No, one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I just want to go to the following day. You indicated that -- that you went for a drive with Sefer Halilovic, which took you to Diva Grabovica and on to Kostajnica. At Diva Grabovica, you indicated that you saw some signs indicating minefields. Did you ever ascertain for your own -- to your own satisfaction precisely where those minefields were?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first and the only time in my life that I was there, I think that there were markings on the sides and somebody said, "Okay, this is a minefield." And we got out of the car. "Are we allowed to go further?" "No." And then Sefer said, "Well, it's a matter of fate," and he set out, and we followed him. And then we went by car even further through the forest to the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. And after that, you went down to Kostajnica. And that's -- and that was where there was a conversation with some refugees from the Capljina area; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, most of them were from Capljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. And I'm not going to take you to sections of your book, but it's -- it's true, isn't it, that it was at that discussion that Sefer made the comment which you tape-recorded live, that "We are not an avenging army"; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: That speech that you heard -- sorry, that -- not speech. I take that back. But those comments that you heard Sefer Halilovic make on that occasion were the typical sort of comments that he would make when speaking in public in situations like that; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whenever I was present, that was a characteristic part of his speech, as it were. And I've had the opportunity to hear it, and I did mention it in the book on several occasions. There were quite a few situations. It seemed to me that he complied with the law even too much, considering the circumstances, especially at the first stage of the war. There was a guy called Juka Prazina. He was a fighter and -- he was a common criminal, actually, to be honest. And he was such a nuisance that some people are saying that he should be killed, liquidated, and gotten rid of. And once talked about these rumours and comments with Sefer and he said, "No, no, no, we can't have that. We have to act in line with the law. The law exists. They can arrest him and then he can be punished. If according to the law he is to be released, okay, but he has to be hanged. He will have to be hanged according to the provisions to have law. But nobody should take it upon themselves to dispense justice."

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I just want to jump forward to the conversation you had with Sefer Halilovic in the car on the way to Dobro Polje, where you asked him about what should be done about the investigation and what he'd discussed with Bakir Alispahic at Konjic. Do you recall that conversation?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. Well, is what he said in the car on that occasion consistent with the stance that you've just described that Sefer Halilovic had towards investigating of criminal matters; namely, that --

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: -- it was important that criminal offences be investigated by the proper organs without interference?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Completely. And it was clear to me and it was quite clear to me that that was what he was like. Always.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And just remaining with that conversation for a minute. Is it the fact that he told you that he'd already tasked the security officer from the inspection team, Namik Dzankovic, to perform exactly that task; namely, to investigate the crime?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He did not mention any names at the time, but he did say, "There are people who are in charge of investigating crime. That's their task."

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And as part of your journalistic work some years later, did you take the opportunity to speak to Namik Dzankovic yourself personally and see what he said about it?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I talked to Dzankovic when I was preparing to write my series, and I asked him and phoned him up and I asked him to meet. And I said, "Now I have to write about this. Did you get any orders from Sefer in relation to the crime?" And he said "Yes." He came to see me in a room with Nedzad and Brankovic. I can't remember the other's name. And he said, "No, no, no. I -- I can't account for that. You have to investigate and do what needs to be done."

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: When you say -- you've just said, "No, no, no. I can't can you tell account for that." Did you mean by that that Halilovic was telling Dzankovic that he, Sefer, did not approve of the crime and was not associated with it?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that he had nothing to do with this crime; in that sense, that he had nothing to do with the crime and that it has nothing to do with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And -- yes, I understand. Okay. Well, now, returning back to the -- to the 3rd of September and the meeting at -- at Kostajnica. Did -- where is Kostajnica? Can you just say what's the nearest military unit to Kostajnica at that time?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At Kostajnica -- no, Buturovic Polje. That was where the 45th Mountain Brigade was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. And that was where the headquarters of Haso Hakalovic was; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, okay. All right. Thank you for that. And some of the refugees at Kostajnica were very emotional and upset and were using terms such as "revenge" during their discussions; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I remember, for example, that a woman said that as many as 11 members of her family had been killed, and there were all sorts of things, even more than I managed to record. But there was a sort of threatening atmosphere.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. And it was in that context that Sefer Halilovic made the -- the comments that you tape-recorded and about which you've given evidence here; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I did report it accurately. I didn't change a single word. I recorded it on a tape. And even when a sentence was kind of hanging in the air and unfinished, I left it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, I understand. All right. Now, I want to turn to the 4th of September, 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, maybe it's time for a break.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We'll take a break, and we'll resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Morrissey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. We've now found the page that -- that -- of the diary that the witness was referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thanks, Mr. Hodzic. What I'm going to do is show you that page that you referred to, and then it might be possible --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: We're just having research done now to see if we could find the date of that. Could that page please be brought up. The diary -- the diary is MFI292. And the page that we want to be shown on the screen is 01057811. But because it's handwritten, I'd also ask, just to assist the witness, that he have a chance of -- to have this -- to have this hard copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: What I'm going to get you to do, when this appears on the screen, Mr. Hodzic, is just to read it out in your own language, just read it live into the transcript so that the interpreters can interpret it for those English speakers present in court.

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I wrote down here, but I can't see the date, unfortunately, so it reads: "Sefer Halilovic is coordinating military operations from Bugojno to Mostar."

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm not getting a translation there, I'm sorry to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: My apologies, Mr. Hodzic. I've got -- I've got earphone troubles, I think. Now it's fixed. All right. And just for completeness, so that the -- the Tribunal has a -- has a clear idea. I think they can possibly read what's above. But if you just read the notes above that on the top half of the page as well just to explain what those are.

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Up here, at the top of the page, I wrote down: "Caco - the 10th Mountain. Celo - the 9th Motorised. Adnan - the 2nd Independent Battalion Sarajevo." I drew a line underneath that and a dash, "Sefer Halilovic coordinating military operations between Bugojno and Mostar." This is my handwriting you can see here. And that's what I jotted down during the actual action, just before combat activities began, in order to know later on in my reports how I would refer to each of these. Sefer told me at the time, "I am the coordinator," and that was the first I heard of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, I understand. All right. Now, in terms of locating the precise date of that -- I understand that you say it was done just before the commencement of combat operations. What may be possible is that during the next break, if you were provided with a copy of -- of -- of your diary in its original form, would you be prepared to just have a look at that page and the pages around it and just see if you're able to work out the precise date from looking like that? Would you be prepared to do that when we have the next break in evidence?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I've looked at it already, and I know exactly what it says there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But as I have already told you, in my diary I would just open a page. Those were difficult times, and I had suffered a trauma myself. The dates may be a bit confusing, and there may be some predating or postdating. As far as I remember, the previous page talks about Dreznica and the fighting at Dreznica. I can't be quite certain about this, but I think this should be after Dreznica, a while after, but I can't be certain about this. I think it was before, actually. I remember when we talked about it, I found that slightly surprising, even shocking, when the -- when he told me this about being coordinator. I thought to myself, He must mean commander. But he said "coordinator," and that's what I recorded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Ms. Chana, are there any objections to furnish the hard copy of this diary during the next break to refresh the memory of this witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Not at all, Your Honour. I will make it available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thanks. I'm grateful to my learned friend for that. Thank you for --

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Sorry, Counsel. In fact, I can assist the Court and I have it available straightaway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I see. But not now. Maybe that will waste a lot of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Well -- Your Honours, what I had in mind was it might -- the witness could do that at his leisure at that time. But I'm grateful to the Prosecutor in any event. Thank you. And that will be done. Very well. So thank you. Your Honours, I offer that separate page as a separate exhibit, bearing in mind that -- the word that's used on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: We think that's -- sorry. Could I just assist -- ask for some assistance.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: MFI293.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: 293. Yes. I'm grateful for that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hodzic. Now, I wanted to -- before the break, we were at September the 4th. And on that day you found -- you indicated that you found yourself sitting at -- outside Dr. Cibo's residence when you know urgent telegram -- is it the fact that on that occasion you were told of an urgent telegram, that it arrived from Mostar, in particular from Arif Pasalic, indicating that there was likely to be a serious offensive by the HVO at some time in the next week?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it said. I got the telegram later from the Bosnia-Herzegovina files, and I included it in my book.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. And to your knowledge, at that time, the HVO leadership had made it quite clear in public that their intention was to establish the capital city of the new state of Herceg-Bosna, indeed in the city of Mostar; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. The capital. That's what they called it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Now, this is not the time to -- for me to ask you the full picture of the situation in Mostar. I just want to ask you two very brief questions, and answer to the -- to the best of your ability, so far as you know the answer to this question. What was the -- what was the humanitarian situation facing civilians of the Bosnian state in the city of Mostar at that time?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't there myself at the time; however, based on what I could glean from media reports and the documents that I had the occasion to inspect in relation to a different series that I published, the situation was critical. It was simply dreadful. The HVO would not allow any humanitarian convoys to get through. That was the situation at the time. It was dreadful. It was hair-raising. And that was the first time I entered Mostar, I think in September 1994. But the town had been destroyed entirely. I had no idea where the people from the eastern part of the town lived. They had no roofs over their heads. It was a -- a catastrophe in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
