utterances.text: Okay. Well, look, bearing in mind you didn't see the town yourself at that time, in September 1993, I won't ask you any further questions about it. But I will ask you this: It appeared to you in your time with Sefer Halilovic that he personally was very concerned and worried about the fate of the civilians in Mostar; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think he had emotional ties to Mostar too. As far as I know, he had spent a long time there as an officer. Secondly, he was facing a dramatic situation. In the war, he entered Mostar as Chief of Staff. And there was some sort of a fluid connection, if I may call it that, between him and the soldiers of Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. And -- yes, I understand. All right. Well, now -- sorry, to continue back to the 4th of September. On that occasion, you indicated that there was a -- a meeting between Commander Delic and his group on the road and Sefer Halilovic and his group. And you indicated that after that meeting, it was agreed that there'd be -- sorry, I take that back. I'll ask the question again. After that roadside meeting, there was then after that a conference that took place down in -- in Zuka's base in Donja Jablanica; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. And an agreement to that effect was -- well, sorry, perhaps I'll -- again, I'll start again. The meeting in Donja Jablanica was agreed upon when you parted company from Delic at that roadside meeting; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, when we were there, not earlier. Before we parted ways, we agreed about this meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. I understand that. And so it was -- and then in the car after the roadside meeting but before the Donja Jablanica meeting, it was then that Sefer made his comment to Dr. Cibo about Delic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Though he made the comment to me too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, I understand. And so that -- the context of the comment was that you were already driving to have a meeting with Commander Delic a little bit later in the morning; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was on our way to Neretvica, and later we would return from Neretvica and go to the meeting. On our way there, near Here, we were looking for the commander of the 6th Corps and another brigade, but we couldn't find either of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. To your observation, the commander of the 6th Corps -- no, I withdraw that. I'll ask you some questions about him a bit later on. Now, I just have a question though quickly about -- about the comment that -- that Sefer Halilovic made to Dr. Cibo and to you concerning what he alleged about Delic. He was telling you that Delic had effectively restricted his power to a -- a management role. Are you able to recall the precise words that he used? If you can't, you can't. But what can you tell us about the actual words he used?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he said something along the following lines: "Delic had received an assignment to take as many powers from me as he could," and that he - that is, Sefer Halilovic - should have under his purview a couple of small things, an administration department, something like that. Nothing major.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, I understand. And in that regard -- I just want to jump forward to something else. You mentioned that at -- at Hrasnica, when you came back out of Sarajevo later on on the -- on the night of the 7th of September, that Sefer on that occasion had trouble arranging trucks and had some trouble persuading Caco to come on the journey. Do you remember that incident?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Is it the fact that Sefer Halilovic appeared to you to have to persuade soldiers to cooperate in the combat actions? I take that back, not soldiers. That Sefer Halilovic had to persuade officers to assist him in the combat operations in which he was involved in Herzegovina at this time?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Obviously, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And it appeared to you that Sefer had to deal with officers by persuasion rather than by the issuing of orders, as a commander normally would do; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. But -- and this may be surprising. It didn't surprise me at the time, though, because that was the situation up until the end of the war in the army. There was no major difference between a commander on the one hand and a soldier on the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Hodzic, we've heard evidence about the theory of how military orders are supposed to be issued by the commander neatly down to a subordinate and then on to other subordinates and so on. But in the real world of the Bosnian army at that time, those leading an operation really had to work by persuading the junior people to do what they were being asked to do, whether it be to go into combat or to perform some other task. Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was the case many times, not only in this particular situation. It was the same in other battles too. Commanders would try to persuade people, but people just refused to do anything about it and the commander would be powerless in these situations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. And certainly in the case of -- the cases of two individuals - and I'm going to mention them, Zuka and Celo - you didn't see Sefer Halilovic issue direct orders to either of those people in the time when you were in -- in Herzegovina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I always say they had their own meetings. I saw him tell Zicro Suljevic to go with Buza. That's one thing I witnessed personally. But I didn't exactly see him give orders to anyone. If I had, I would have recorded it. I would have taken footage and I could show it to you now. But I have no idea what happened -- what was happening behind closed doors at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Of course. And I'm not asking you to speculate about those matters but simply to comment, as you have, on what you saw yourself. And I should just ask you this question: Did you ever see any person issue a direct order to Ramiz Delalic, Celo? And I'll -- well, I'll ask you that question first and then I've got one afterwards.

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, certainly not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And just based on what you observed, would that have been a very realistic thing to do, based on your knowledge of Ramiz Delalic, Celo?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid I don't understand your question. What exactly do you mean? Would it have been realistic for someone to order Ramiz Delalic about? Is that what you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... yes.

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no idea who it could have been. He was subordinated to the 1st Corps. I met him there a couple of times. He would come there. I have no idea what they did [as interpreted]. Specifically he asked for reinforcements for the officers to be sent over. I did go to his brigade a couple of times in my capacity as journalist. I saw soldiers heading for the front line. The situation was critical. But I didn't hear anything special about Celo at the time. All the bad things I heard about him were in relation to a Serb that he had killed at the beginning of the war who was in the middle of a wedding ceremony. If you could please specify or substantiate, because I still don't think I entirely understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Look, it was really a very impressionistic question, frankly. And I think you've had two bona fide tries at answering it, so I won't persist any further with it. I should ask you -- you've mentioned that you saw Sefer Halilovic give an order to Zicro Suljevic to go with -- with Buza. Did you ever see the order creating the inspection team?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I see. And when did you see that? Did you see that when you were down in Herzegovina or later on, when you were doing research?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I had no idea about that order. It was later when I obtained a copy from the archives.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Okay.

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During my research.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, I won't press you about that any further, if that's the case as well. Very well. Thank you. Well, now, I had jumped forward there, but at this stage I -- we were back on the 4th of September. You've indicated that you didn't attend the -- the meeting at Donja Jablanica, but it's the fact, isn't it, that Delic, Sefer and a number of other commanders attended a meeting at Donja Jablanica later on on the 4th and that they stayed in that meeting for over an hour discussing various matters; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no idea what they discussed. I didn't hear anything about that. They were there. They talked. They had a meeting. Once the meeting was over, I took a brief statement from Delic and we were on our way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Could I ask you -- you may recall this; you may not. Did you ever see a map that was signed by both Commander Delic and Chief of Staff, Halilovic, after -- after that meeting?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't see a map. The first time I saw it was after the war. It was published in a Sarajevo newspaper. Just in the heading they showed perhaps half the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. And look, I -- I think perhaps this will save some time for later on. There's just a couple of documents. I want to ask you whether you saw them at the time. You may have, you may not, and you can tell us. Did you see when you were still down in Herzegovina a combat order headed "Defence of People's Rights, Vrdi 93," a combat order dated the 11th of September and signed by Zulfikar Alispago?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember having seen that. I don't think I ever obtained it at any of the later stages and I certainly don't have it on my now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: No, no, that's okay. And I'm not suggesting that you should have had it. Was it the practice of any of the commanders in Herzegovina when you were down there to show you the combat orders, or not?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No one ever showed me anything. Not Sefer, not anyone else. I'm not sure who would have been entitled to show me anything, including Karic and the rest of them. Well, actually, Sefer did show me things two or three times, but I never actually held any of these in my own hands, not any of the orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And just with particular reference to that, you didn't see the map at -- at that time -- well, sorry. I think you've answered that question already. Very well. I can move now to the 5th of -- of September and just ask you: At approximately what time did you set off to go back to Sarajevo after that Dobro Polje meeting which you've given evidence about?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say when specifically we set off. It was in the evening. I can't say what time it was. But we reached a fountain near a Croatian village. I'm not sure what the name of the village was. We would always stop there on our way from Jablanica to Sarajevo and the other way around. The water in that well was lovely and cold. There was an apple tree with ripe apples on it, and then 20 metres down there was a group of houses all grouped together. We arrived from Dobro Polje and we stopped there, as we always did. I saw that a light was on in one of the houses, an oil lamp, actually. We set off from Dobro Polje for Sarajevo on a moment's notice and we always tried to bring food back to Sarajevo because it cost an arm and a leg in Sarajevo and over there everything was cheap. I tried to get some cheese, because the discrepancy in the prices was enormous. In Sarajevo, it cost between 30 and 40 Deutschmark, and over there it was just 2. I told Sefer, "Please, can you just wait a minute? I'm going to that house over there where you can see the lamp burning. I'll ask them whether they have any cheese to sell." And he said, "What's the matter with you? It's past 10.00. It's late. No time for that." I was wearing a camouflage jacket, and he said, "If you show up at their door in a uniform like this and those people over there are Croats, you'll frighten those poor people out of their wits. You won't achieve anything. They will give it to you for nothing. But I advise you not to go. Just let the people sleep. Don't disturb them." So we were at the well. It was past 10.00. And I can't remember specifically when we left the place. So I decided not to go down to the house and we just pressed on back to Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. Thanks. Now, I won't ask you any questions about what happened in Sarajevo. And I want to just move quickly now to the 7th of September at Hrasnica, and just to ask you -- ask for a couple of clarifications about what happened there. The procedure was to get to Hrasnica that you went and met Sefer at a headquarters; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We met at his headquarters in Sarajevo and then we went to Hrasnica together.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And we went again together.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. No, sorry, I -- I must have been misleading, because that's what I meant. And when you went there to meet him, did you observe Ramiz Delalic to be present at the headquarters when you got there?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I met him in the corridor, and I asked him whether he was going as well, and that's when I found out he was, and his unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. And then did he -- did Ramiz Delalic travel to the tunnel with you, or did he go another way?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. I mean, incidentally, although a lot of things are said about Ramiz Delalic, the fact is in the defence of Sarajevo he was a very brave fighter who defended a very important part of the front line; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. His men and he himself were really at a very important -- a long very important line from Miljacka northwards to the north-east of the city. And I must say that I once had the opportunity to go there and to see how those fighters at a critical time, when they were closing off that area and the Serb lines -- the Serb forces were advancing, and then there was a break in these lines in the defence, and he sent these really courageous, brave people there. And there was a really nice atmosphere, and they managed to close ranks and they defended the area. And I think it was in -- and he had a very good relationship with these people and he talked to them nicely and he said, "Are you okay? Hurry up." I mean, I couldn't see anything bad about the person at all when I was there. Afterwards I did hear stuff, but I have seen no nasty things firsthand.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: No. And just one final question about that, that -- that Ramiz Delalic was plainly a person who took a very hands-on interest in the well-being of his soldiers when you were there present with him; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And I think Caco was one of the best ones in that respect as well. They took special care of their soldiers. I don't know about Celo, but Caco -- I know some relatives of mine used to live there. And -- well, he did it in a strange way, but he did care about people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. Now, I just want to take you to -- take you to Hrasnica. You travelled to the tunnel and you went through the tunnel, and then you found yourself out of Sarajevo and at the forward command post of the 1st Corps in the Hrasnica area. Now, could I just ask you this: Fikret Prevljak was a person who was the commander of the local brigade stationed outside Sarajevo in and around Hrasnica; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the 4th Motorised Brigade, and he was the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I understand. Now, I just want to clarify something that -- that my learned friend asked you yesterday. You indicated that -- that when you and Sefer arrived there, there was some news that Caco was not going to come. Is that correct? Or that he was refusing to come to Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. And at that point, Sefer Halilovic tried to persuade Ramiz Delalic to go and help him get Caco to come; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And ultimately Sefer Halilovic succeeded in persuading Caco to do that and the two of them set off; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. But they didn't have to go back into Sarajevo through the tunnel, did they, as far as you knew? They just had to go somewhere else in the area of Hrasnica to find Caco; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Chana.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Counsel, I think there is -- you said "Caco" when I think you meant Celo, the two of them set off. Line 20, 11:34.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I might have a different numbering system from my friend. I'll just make sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And ultimately --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. No, no, yes, my friend is right there. Yes, okay. I can recollect that. It's line 13, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I -- I made a technical mistake there. I think you probably understood it the right way, Mr. Hodzic, but I'll just put it anyway. Firstly, you've already said that Sefer tried to persuade Ramiz Delalic to get Caco to come. And then after that, Sefer Halilovic did persuade Celo to help and the two of them set off. And you've said -- sorry, is that correct? I just have to ask -- get you to answer that one, because it's been --

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you. Okay. And after they left -- so we have Sefer and -- and Ramiz Delalic leaving to go to find Caco. And to your knowledge, they were looking in the area of Hrasnica, where Caco already was; correct?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: So to your understanding, the situation that Halilovic was trying to resolve was this one: Soldiers had already come from Sarajevo with Caco and come to Hrasnica, but now on the eve of departing Caco was talking about going back to Sarajevo; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it could be concluded on the basis of what we had heard there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Now, I understand that you were going on what you were told. Of course. How long did it take before Ramiz Delalic -- well, first of all, did Ramiz Delalic and Sefer Halilovic come back together or separately?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know. I really don't know whether they were together or not. But they certainly left together.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. I understand. Very well. And then -- and how long was it that they were gone? I understand you may not be able to give us a minute-perfect answer, but were they gone for 20 minutes or an hour? What -- what sort of range?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's hard for me to say. I really did not pay much attention. Perhaps 20 minutes. Perhaps 15. Perhaps half an hour. I don't know. It's speculation only. I can't really say anything. But after a little bit of time, Sefer came back, and I suppose Celo as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. Well, look, thank you for trying. I understand some of these questions might be asking for detail that's too far away. Very well. Well, now, I'm not going to ask you any questions about the journey down to -- to Jablanica. And I want to move forward now to the time when you saw Sefer Halilovic after you'd already heard the horrible rumours that you'd already heard about -- about Grabovica. Now, you indicated that you saw Sefer Halilovic while you were sitting on chairs, and I think you said at Zuka's base. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I got there before he did, and then he joined me soon afterwards. He sat next to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. I understand that. And the conditions were not possible for you to hold a -- a conversation with him on this topic because there were many soldiers around; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. It's a very small -- a small room.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. But so far as you could judge, Sefer Halilovic appeared to be visibly shaken and shocked by the news that you'd both received coming out of Grabovica; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it is a bit difficult now, but yes, he was really absent -- how should I put this? I thought of the right word when Ms. Chana asked me this question. He was quiet. And something else I wanted to say, something more accurate: He was more than just quiet. He was pensive, not just quiet.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, I understand. How long do you think you were with him on that occasion? Was it a matter of two minutes or five minutes or -- or a significantly longer time than that?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very briefly, just to say that he was in the direction of Konjic, that he was with Mahmutcehajic. And when I asked him about whether he had heard about this, and I asked him in a very low voice, and he said, "Yes." And I asked him, "Do you think that it may be one of the refugees that may be the killer?" And he said, "Yes." And the others joined us. And it was mostly the same whenever he came.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, I understand. All right. Now, I just want to move on to the next morning, the 10th, the morning of the 10th of September, and ask you some questions about the arrival of Ramiz Delalic on -- on that morning. Now, I think your evidence was that you were hoping to get a lift from somebody who went past, because you didn't have your own vehicle, and you were just seated hoping someone would come by.

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. So when -- when the car pulled up driven by Ramiz Delalic, can you recall where it parked? Did it park right up against the houses or did it park -- the houses of Zuka's base or did it park some distance away from those houses?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right in front of the building, in the middle of the road. Nothing -- no traffic would be disturbed. Because for about half an hour, an hour, no car would drive by. And it was right across the street from Zuka's base.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. So are you able to say approximately -- this is getting a little bit -- a bit difficult; but I just ask you to do the best you can. Could you estimate how many metres away from the front steps of Zuka's base this car was parked? Just doing the best you can.

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe it was further than 5 metres away.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, can you just indicate to the Tribunal what sort of vehicle was it? Was it a jeep or was it an Audi? What was it?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I can't remember. I can't really say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Can you recall whether or not it was a military vehicle or a civilian vehicle?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say that either.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you saw Ramiz Delalic exit the -- the vehicle. At the time he exited the vehicle, was there any other person, apart from the two boys, in the vehicle that you could see?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was this driver. The driver was there. Celo wasn't driving.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I understand. Do you recall the name of that particular driver that you saw?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say whether it was him on that particular occasion, but the one who drove him most often. He almost always drove him. And I keep meeting him all over Sarajevo, because he's a taxi driver in Sarajevo at the moment. But I can't remember -- maybe Arnautovic Erdin, Arnatalic. I can't remember. I know him. I say hello to him. But I don't know what's his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. So could -- if I refresh your memory by mentioning the name Erdin Arnautovic, that's the person who --

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe he was his permanent driver.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And he must have been there at -- on that occasion as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, just referring to that particular occasion, you indicated earlier on you weren't sure whether he was the driver on that day. Do you have a specific memory of it being him that day or not?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I can't remember. I wasn't really paying attention. But there was a driver, some driver.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. And for how long did the boys stay in the car before Ramiz came back and got them?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is hard to say. I mean, Celo didn't come in and go straight back out, but he talked to Nihad Bojadzic and the deputy commander. It wasn't a very long conversation, but I looked in and I saw them still talking. I am afraid I might make a mistake here. Whatever I tell you, how many minutes, two, three, five. I really don't want to make a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: That's okay. I -- I think you've made yourself very clear about it. Just to explain to the Tribunal who Nihad Bojadzic is. Nihad Bojadzic was the deputy commander of Zulfikar Alispago's unit; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. And he's a person who played a leading part in the fighting down in Dreznica in the following week or so; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think he was in charge of that at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. So were you able to observe the demeanour of the two men, Bojadzic and Ramiz Delalic, during the time of this short conversation?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't have the opportunity to, but I was sitting outside. I was sitting on a chair facing the street. And they were indoors and there was a kind of bar, a table. And I was in a hurry and I was looking for Celo and they were still talking. But then he came out again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. Thank you. And -- and thereafter you got a lift with Mr. Delalic not yet knowing who those boys were; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I thought some of the refugee children, some poor devils that he was taking to Jablanica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Just -- from the position that you were in, sitting outside of the restaurant -- sorry, I take that back, "restaurant." I've got that on the brain. Mr. Hodzic, I'm sorry. Sitting outside as you were, you were not in a position to overhear the conversation that took place between Ramiz and -- and Nihad Bojadzic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, absolutely not. I didn't hear a single word.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And during the time when they were inside, did the driver of the car appear to you to stay seated inside that car with the boys?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he had stayed in the car. And he certainly did not go in.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't remember, by the way. But I -- I don't think he went in.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And he certainly didn't come and sit with you where you were sitting; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. Thanks. Now, the next matter I want to take you to is that? In due course -- sorry, I asked you about this earlier on. So I now want to move forward to the time when you found yourself in the car talking to Sefer Halilovic about what should be done in respect of this investigation. And I've already asked you some questions about that earlier on, so these -- these will now be very quick. At the time when you were in that vehicle and that conversation took place, who else was in the car with you? Was -- was Dr. Cibo in the car on that occasion or was there any other person in the car with you on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Cibo, the driver, this person called Mesar who was driving, and the escorts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sefer's brother and his son, I believe. That was it. And apart from this entourage, Cibo and myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. There's been quite a few mentions in passing about Sefer's son. And perhaps you can clarify what the situation was there. To your understanding, when Sefer came down to Herzegovina, did he bring with him his son, whose name is Semir?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he always brought him with him, and he never separated from him, and he never wanted to be away from him. It is a kind of a mystery to me even now, because we had some very risky trips, actually, and we were risking our lives. We could have been hit by a bullet or we could have ended up off the road on those mountain roads. But he always took him along.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. I suppose you could perhaps comment on this: Did it come to your knowledge that Semir Halilovic, Sefer's son, was actually in the flat when his mother was blown to pieces?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I read that in Sefer's book.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And to your observation, Sefer wanted to keep Semir in eye contact all the time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never asked him about that, I must admit. I felt uncomfortable about asking about it. But it was a bit of a mystery. Why does he insist on taking a 13-year-old boy to such risky trips. I don't know. It was obvious that he wanted to be with him. But I couldn't really guess what was in his mind. But it was surprising, because I had never witnessed anything like that in the war. There were commanders who brought their sons along as escorts. Delic used to do that, and Sefer took his brother, and Karic's son was with him most of the time in the course of operation. But for a 12- or 13-year-old boy to be taken along, it has still remained a mystery. It is even a mystery to me now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Just on the topic that you raised then, did you meet Vehbija Karic's son in the course of your time in Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite a few times, and it was precisely to him that I gave the pictures on the 8th of November when we came back and we went to Donja Jablanica in front of the base, when Karic, Bilajac, and Zicro came, and I think there was somebody else there called Sokolo [phoen] or something like that. And I was circulating pictures that I brought along. And I gave them to this boy -- well, a young man. And he said to me, "Well, you'll see this is going to be quite something. We are preparing this operation." He was with his father all the time, and I had known him from before, from Sarajevo. I think I had met him in June.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. And was it within your knowledge that the wife of Vehbija Karic and the mother of this young boy was Croatian?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I found out in a weird way. It is not unusual to see mixed marriages back home, but I found out about three weeks after we came back, some days after the start of the Trebevic operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was at Karic's place, in case you're interested in this story.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Just -- it's really the question of whether you knew that as a fact or not. I won't trouble you with the -- with the history of it.

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is important.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, sorry, no, if you think -- look, I'll press on with the questions in regard to that. Sorry, just bearing in mind the time, I must say. I'm torn. I'm torn, actually. But look, anyway, I will press on. Sorry. Look, if you see it as a matter of importance, perhaps you should say what -- what you have to say about that.

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. I came to Karic's place precisely on the day when some international agency broadcasted news that Sefer Halilovic was under house arrest, and I think it was also mentioned on the radio. And there was information from the Chief of Staff [as interpreted] that he wasn't, and we knew that he was, and so I came to Karic's place and I asked him -- I told him that -- is it true that Sefer is under house arrest and that there was some mistreatment in the State Security Service? And then I said, "Well, he had some problems." And I asked, "Did you have any problems?" And he said, "Yes, yes, I had problems." And that was the occasion when he told me -- he said, "Jusuf Jasarevic asked me to make a statement because those people down there" -- I'm not really going to use the word that he used. I might make a mistake, but at any rate, "These people who killed those people down in Grabovica said that I had told them if they don't give you accommodation, throw them into the river, into Neretva." And I couldn't say that ever. Apart from that, my son was there. And my wife is Croatian, and that's how I found out that she was Croatian. And he said, "She's half Croatian and there's no way I could say that in front of my son. His grandmother and grandfather are Croats and I couldn't say, "Go ahead and kill those Croats." That's how I found out, and I think that's a pretty important point.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I think you're right. Thank you for the explanation. Okay. Well, there's -- sorry, there's just --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, there's just a translation issue that I need to raise there. At line 5, the interpretation says, starting at line 4: "And there was information from the Chief of Staff that he wasn't." And we are advised by the Bosnian speaker at the table that the word used there was not "Chief of Staff" but "Main Staff." And I just ask for a clarification on that point, if possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, please. Well, you may ask a question to this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, as sometimes happens with me, I talk too much and then the phrase disappears at the top of the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I just want to clarify one part of your evidence there. You said this - and I'm just going to ask for a comment on one point - you said this: "I came to Karic's place precisely on the day when some international agency broadcasted news that Sefer Halilovic was under house arrest. And I think it was also mentioned on the radio. And there was information from the Chief of Staff that he wasn't." Now, we've got on our screen that "there was information from the Chief of Staff that he wasn't." Did you mean to say "the Chief of Staff" or did you mean to say "there was information from the Main Staff that he wasn't"?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no, it wasn't from the Chief of Staff. The army came along. But it came from the army. They denied this information, that -- they said that Sefer Halilovic was not under house arrest. Of course we laughed at it because we knew that he was. Karic spoke to him on the phone that very day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And just to clarify two matters there. As to the names of the people who were accusing Karic, did Karic say who it was that was pointing the finger at him as to making this comment, or did he not give you that information?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Once again, I am afraid I might use a wrong word here, something he didn't say, so I'm going to paraphrase it. He said to me, yes, that he had problems as well. He had a call from the general -- no, he wasn't the general -- from Jusuf Jasarevic to clarify some things and to make a statement. And then he found out that those who perpetrated the crimes at Grabovica accused him by saying that he had told them, "Okay, if you are not given accommodation, just throw these people into the river." And he said that there was no problem with accommodation. He said that to me as well. And that everything was fine. And he said, "Bilajac was down there and they were sitting together with these people and apparently Bilajac got some garlic from some Croats and the army and all of them were talking to them, with these Croats, and there were no problems there, and there's no way he could have said that. And then he went on to say, "Well, my son was standing next to me, and he's half Croat, half Bosnian, because my wife, his mother, is Croatian and his grandparents are Croatian, and how could I say that?"

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. Yes. Well, thank you very much for that clarification. Now I want to ask you some questions about the document that Sefer Halilovic read out to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I just inquire when Your Honours would be inclined to take the break? I think it's likely that I would go into the extra session, if that's needed. I also think it's likely that we would -- if that's available still. And I think it's likely that I would finish in that time. But can I just -- just so that I know how to manage the time now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I'm at your disposal. If you believe that it's the right time for us to take a break, we could.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, it would help me just to organise now because -- that would help.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: The courtroom for this afternoon's sitting is reserved already, so there's no problem on that. Yes. We'll resume at 12.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Morrissey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thanks, Mr. Hodzic. I've now got some questions concerning the conversation that you had with Sefer Halilovic when he indicated a particular telegram that was sent to you and he read to you a -- a passage from that telegram. Now, first of all, the questions I'm going to ask you concern a particular document, and that's the document that you were shown by the Prosecutor which you indicated had been given to you in archives a long time later. So I'm going to show you the document and -- and then I'll ask you some preliminary questions about it. But perhaps if the document could be brought up now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: It's MFI259. I think it is. Sorry, excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: No, no, no, it's not to be do with MFI259. It's D157. My apologies for that. I just saw the "259" notation on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Now, the document I'm going to show you now is a document that you were shown earlier on. It's a document that -- it purports to be an order from Komandant Rasim Delic dated 12/9/1993. Now, just tell us when you have that on the screen, if you wouldn't mind.

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. Thanks. Now, just -- just before I come to the -- the text of it, I'll tell you frankly so there's no sneakiness about, this I've just got some questions about some of the times down -- down at the bottom on this particular piece of paper. But first questions are just general ones. To the best of your recollection, you -- you've indicated here that -- that Mr. Halilovic produced a piece of paper in the car and he read out some words from that -- from that piece of paper to you, but you didn't have your glasses on, so you couldn't read it. Is that correct? Have I got it right, what you said?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it wasn't in the car. It was outside Zuka's base.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We headed for the car, and it was before we got into the car. It's true, however, that I was unable to read this. I had forgotten to put my glasses on. It's as simple as that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, that's okay. I'm just -- what I'm going to be asking you is when you first actually saw this particular document, which -- which has been put into evidence here. Now -- and so I'm going to trace through what you actually saw on the day of the 12th. What you saw outside Zuka's base was a piece of paper, and you heard Sefer Halilovic reading out certain things to you from that piece of paper. Is that -- is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. And what he read out to you was that -- the passage which said: "Re-examine the decision in the sense of a realistic estimate of forces and possibilities of carrying out the tasks in accordance with that. Amend the decision so it conforms to real possibilities." Is that what he read out to you, the words that I've just stated?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. That section, thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. As I understand.

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall it word by word right now, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: No, of course not. I understand that. But at that time, Sefer Halilovic read out nothing to do with any checking of the accuracy of information about genocide committed against civilian population by members of the 1st Corps 9th Mountain Brigade. At that time, and in relation to this piece of paper that you saw, Sefer Halilovic said nothing about Grabovica; is that accurate as well?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he didn't say anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I understand. Okay. Now, the next -- I'm just -- this is just chasing -- tracing through what you saw on the day. After that, did you see that piece of paper again that Sefer Halilovic had?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Never.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, however, when you got up to the northern front or the northern part of the lines, you saw Vehbija Karic, and he also mentioned receiving -- mentioned to Sefer Halilovic receiving some sort of telegram as well; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I understand. Okay. And -- but on that occasion, you didn't see any piece of paper in Vehbija Karic's hands, did you?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. And -- all right. And after the discussion between Vehbija Karic and Sefer on that occasion, there was no -- okay. Well, I'll stop there. Now, the reason I ask this is because I just want to put to you the possibility that the -- the document that you were shown later from the archives might turn out not to be the original one. Now, I don't know. But I'm going to give you the chance to comment about that. And -- and I'm going to show you some things on the document. So there's no trickery here, and I just want you to be able -- you say whatever you have to say about this. Would you mind just having a look, please, at the -- at the marks at the bottom of that document there, the stamps of when things were sent and when they were received and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, what's being shown -- on the English version -- Sorry, just excuse me, Mr. Hodzic. On the English version that you have before you on the screen, it's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: No. I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: What I'm going to do is ask that the Bosnian version be displayed -- sorry, would you just excuse me a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, sorry. Pardon me. I'm just going to ask that the Bosnian version be displayed to all in court so that you can see what's being pointed out to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: What I'm going to ask you about is the timing here, Mr. Hodzic, because it just looks as if this particular document that I've got in my hands just doesn't appear to have been sent down to Jablanica until much later in the day. And so for that reason I'm just going to ask you, and any comment you've got to make, feel free. Do you see on the left there there's a stamp indicating the arrival of this document on the 12th of the 9th, 1993 at 14.14 hours? Can you see that on the bottom left?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. And just from your recollection, you had well and truly left Jablanica by the time 14.14 hours came along, hadn't you?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At about 10.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, I understand.

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps even earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, just -- just thinking about that. When you were shown this particular document when you went back to the archives, how did it come to be in your hands? Was it given to you by archivist, or did you have to write a letter? Can you just explain how it came about?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I filed a request in writing, and I was given the documents. I didn't physically search the archive to locate these documents myself. I requested both documents when I was preparing a series for my newspaper. The request was approved, and the chief of cabinet of Rasim Delic told me that it would be okay and that there were some other things that he had for me but they didn't give these to me after all for my series. It was only a good while later that I was able to convince them to -- to hand them over. But as far as my experience in the archives is concerned, this document appears to be accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. No, that's okay. Do you remember, was it the original document -- was the document that you received a copy, or was it an original?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. It's hard for me to say. It must have been a copy. I suppose it couldn't have been the original. I would not have been allowed to take the original from the archive and take it away. Not a chance.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: No, well, that's -- I mean, I'm very much in your hands here about the procedures there, Mr. Hodzic, and I'm grateful for the explanations. Now, there's no criticism at all being made of you about this. I just wonder if you can think of any explanation as to how this would happen, that this would -- sorry, there's an objection coming, so ...?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I think Counsel knows what my objection is. The witness has very clearly stated he never saw this document. He can hardly now be asked to look at the -- the stamps. He may be asked what time he left. Yes, that's fine. As it reflects on the document. But the witness cannot answer these questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Maybe the witness is not in the good position to make any comments as for those stamps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I think, with the greatest sadness, I think my learned friend is right. I don't think this witness can comment any further than he has.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Perhaps I'll just ask -- I'll ask one question about it: When you came to inspect this document during the -- during your writing of your book, it wasn't a matter that concerned you to look at these stamps; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Why would I want to waste time on something like that? But I really did use these little things, the small print, and I often compared them, but I'm not sure about the copy I received them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: No, that's okay. I understand. But when you received this document, when you ultimately got your copy of it that was provided for you, that's the first time you'd seen or heard of paragraph 2, the part that contains the reference to Grabovica; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember. That was a long time ago. But I can explain how the misunderstanding came about. I think I was wrong about the date, because after all, once I wrote down the series of articles, I tried to recall things clearly, and there was a discrepancy that occurred to me at that point because I think the next day Karic told Sefer, in my book at least, "There's something for you," and this probably indicates that Sefer showed this to me on the 13th. And I'm very grateful to you for this because it's only now that I realise how I got the dates wrong. It must be a different date. That is it. That's the explanation that we're seeking.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: No, that's okay. All right. Well, thank you for that. Now, I just want to ask you questions about the -- what the news was that you got about the Uzdol events. So we're now jumping forward from the -- from the 13th. You've answered questions asked of you by the -- by the learned Prosecutor. You indicated that combat started on the 13th in that area and that Sefer Halilovic ordered Suljevic to go with Buza and accompany him after finding out that Buza had not gone into action, as he was supposed to do. And then you said that on the 14th you went with Sefer and you went to a communications centre and heard certain news. And the Prosecutor asked you about that, and now I'm just going to ask you to clarify something. At the time when you attended at that communications centre, and -- and heard the news about the fighting in Uzdol, there was no story whatsoever that old civilians or young children had been killed; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Because if there was any such material, you would have, of course, made further inquiries about it; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume so. Nothing was said about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I understand that. Now, some days later, you became aware of reports in the media - and you've described that you were at somebody's house when -- when you learned about those reports in the media - that there may have been crimes committed in -- in Uzdol. And I wanted to ask you about the believability of these reports in the media. First of all, at the time when -- when you learned about these -- the rumours or the stories in the media about killings at Uzdol, were you told that Croat media had featured photographs of bodies lying in the snow, in snow-covered fields?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that, or I don't remember. It was later that I heard people talk about this, and I can remember specifically whether I'd seen snow myself when I saw the reports on TV, but there was someone -- or rather, who told me -- but I'm not sure how to put it. A crime occurred, after all. They said that this was probably fabrication and that some Bosnian bodies of people who had been killed earlier on were being shown. The massacre story was a different story altogether. For example, when my series came out in 1999, someone or other from the army had a reaction but they couldn't really say if the crime in Uzdol happened. It was like this: They couldn't be very specific about it. Until the book on the crime came out, I wasn't sure myself. It came out about three or four years ago. I had a look, and --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness didn't get the last part of the -- Or the interpreter didn't get the last part of the interpreter's answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Hodzic. The interpreter just lost you there. You were a bit fast for him at the end. Would you mind just saying that last part again so that the interpreter catches it.

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until as late as four years ago, which is when the book came out on the crime at Uzdol with photographs, I, or the general public in Bosnia-Herzegovina, had no idea whether the crime really occurred or not. It was only once I had bought the book that I realised the full extent.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Now, that book that you're referring to now was a publication concerning Uzdol that specified the victims and so on; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There's not only that one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Oh, no, I understand that. I'm really talk about back at the time when -- when the rumours first started. You mentioned in evidence earlier on that -- the mention of the word "snow" in connection with these reports, and I just wonder if you could explain to the Tribunal what you meant by that. What did snow have to do with these rumours that you heard?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Allegedly this was in September. There couldn't have been any snow on the ground at this time. It was a nice day, beautiful weather, sunny. You can see the photographs with snow on the ground. This is impossible. It must have been fabricated in some way. Or at least rumour had it that the photographs had been fabricated and that no crime had occurred. That was the general drift. I think Zicro Suljevic gave an interview explaining more or less the same thing, that no crime had in fact occurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. And just as a journalist and a person participating in the media at the time, within your knowledge did media from the Herceg-Bosna side, or the -- well, I don't want to call it the Croatian -- the Croat side, but from the Herceg-Bosna side -- did media from that side sometimes appear to exaggerate or even invent atrocities by the Bosnian government army or by Muslims generally?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: How should I put this? I really can't say. There was a lot of propaganda involved. Some people were saying things, but I spent most of my time at the front lines and I didn't really follow the media closely for the simple reason that I spent most of my time on the ground, so I can't say. I imagine there was a good deal of that around, propaganda quite thick on the ground, but I really can't vouch for anything. I can't be pushed to say anything definite about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: No, I understand. No, well, thanks for that indication. I won't push you any further on that topic at all. I just want to ask you one more question about the -- the lead-up to the Uzdol fighting and the fights on that front generally, at Crni Vrh and other places like that. Were you present when Sefer Halilovic addressed the soldiers of the Independent Prozor Battalion before the fighting at Uzdol?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was there every time he spoke: The time he spoke to the Prozor Battalion, the time he spoke to the Neretva Battalion. It was a battalion, the Neretvica Battalion. All of these. He spoke to people two or three times.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. And as to the speech that he made -- well, I suppose the speeches generally up there I'll ask you about and then I'll ask you specifically. In those speeches, did Sefer Halilovic refer to the fact that they shouldn't be killing civilians and indeed they should be careful of civilians and prisoners of war during their operations?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I did say so yesterday. He was very clear about that. But I can't remember anything else specifically. There must be dozens of people who were there and who remember everything exactly word for word. There was one group he addressed and he made this clear in no uncertain terms. He said the same thing he had said in Kostajnica on the 3rd of September, 1993. He said, "We should not touch civilians. Our army mustn't touch any civilians. It's the Chetniks and Ustashas that we're fighting." He repeated this word for word on the other occasion, but I couldn't get this on tape, simply because I'd run out of tapes by this time. It did occur to me at the time, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, I understand. And that expression about not touching civilians and so on and --

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: That really was -- because you had spoken about his political position, that statement of not touching civilians was particularly consistent with Sefer Halilovic's own commitment to the political solution of a multi-ethnic, unified Bosnia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's difficult for me to say if it's consistent with this or not. As I've told you, I went through the archives. There are quite many orders issued by General Halilovic that seems to be very much in compliance with this principle and respectful of these principles, but same applies to Delic. This was a trend, so to speak, throughout the army, from the very beginning to the very end.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I understand what you say. Very well. Now, you've already given evidence in fairly complete form about -- about what occurred after that time. I just want to go very briefly for a survey just to preserve the chronology for the -- for the Tribunal here. After the Independent Prozor Battalion came back, having been to Uzdol and come back, do you recall there being -- do you recall attending at Voljevac after that time when soldiers of -- of those other -- other units were expressing some resentment and dislike against Enver Buza because of the lateness of the Independent Prozor Battalion? I'm talking now really about the afternoon of the 14th.

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I described this in some detail. They were furious. They were mad. One of their favourite commanders had been killed, the deputy commander, Seid Padalovc. They abandoned the lines for that reason, the lot of them, and they all wanted to go to his funeral. They gathered on a piece of flat ground, a plateau, and they expressed so much anger in fact at Buza's expense. So the first question that was addressed to Sefer when he arrived was: When is -- when will Mehmed Buza [as interpreted] be shot? So that's what I wrote down at the moment, that Buza should go to Voljevac and report on his actions. Every time a car passed by, I feared that Buza would be taken away. No chance he would have survived. I think Sefer and Haso Sakovic [as interpreted] would have done him in [Realtime transcript read in error: "any more"] right there. But this was the report that I published at that time and I have nothing new to add. That was the impression that I had at the time. Fortunately, he never turned up. We didn't see him on that day. We eventually left Voljevac, we left Prozor, and we drove back.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. The transcript here is recorded that you said Haso Sakovic. But you said the words Haso Hakalovic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Haso Hakalovic, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: There is -- sorry, Counsel. I think he said "would have done him in," not "done any more right there." "Would have done him in."

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I'll clarify if, if you like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, sorry. Pardon me. You made a comment at the end of that and the transcript here has recorded you as saying that Haso -- I think it's Sefer -- "Haso Sakovic [sic] would have done any more right there." Could you just explain what you said and what you meant there because there may be a transcript problem; there may not be.

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those soldiers were so furious. They were driven mad. They were to be sent back to the front lines. So Hakalovic spoke to him to calm them down, and Sefer did too. He managed to a certain extent to talk sense to them. It was a very shocking situation. Yet again, Zejnilagic's men referred from another unit, from the lines they had reached the day before, and we were back to square one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I just have -- this -- I've got to ask you a question about a military matter here. You may have been told about it; you may not have been. I'll ask you and you can tell us. Were you aware of whether Vehbija Karic and then subsequently confirmed by Sefer Halilovic issued an order that from that time on the combat operations on that area were to be conducted by Mr. Zejnilagic?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the first I hear of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. Well, if that's the case, I won't press you about it. In the time of your involvement in that area, the Voljevac-Dobro Polje -- the northern part of the operation, if one could use that term, in that time did you notice the -- the frequent presence of Braco Fazlic, the deputy of the -- of the 6th Corps?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was the deputy. He was up there. I saw him. I know for sure that I saw him once, maybe twice. We were at Voljevac together, at Dobro Polje. And since I know Braco quite well from Sarajevo, I could have met him many more times. But those two times I remember specifically.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And I just -- just want to clarify this. At the time when you saw Braco Fazlic up at -- I'm speaking now of the day that combat commenced, the 13th of the 9th. And, in fact, perhaps I'm really asking about three days, the 11th, 12th, and 13th of September. On any of those days, apart from Braco Fazlic, do you recall whether or not you saw Salko Gusic in that area of Voljevac, Dobro Polje, and generally the northern front?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Gusic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Gusic, yes.

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that he was there on that day. Maybe he was, but I am not sure. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. All right. Well, thank you for that. Now, I promised to get on to the 16th of September and the subsequent days. After those problems on the afternoon of the 14th that you've indicated, did you become aware that combat operations were finally beginning at the very south of the operation, in the Vrdi, Dreznica sort of area?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was down there. I followed the combat operations throughout the night. And on the day after, I talked to the fighters who were coming back and I was making the -- recordings and I heard orders being issued through the liaison centre from Zuka and the others. So I followed everything from Dreznica very closely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, I understand. Now, I won't trouble you with -- you've already indicated what -- or the relevant parts of all of that evidence. And I just wanted to ask you this: The combat activities, at least the offensive activities, ceased very suddenly at the end of the 19th of -- of September and were followed by the -- the -- by the return -- or sorry, I'm asking two questions there. Perhaps I'll just ask you that first bit first. The combat activities ceased on the 19th of September; is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And as far as you know, straightaway the Sarajevo units went back to Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether they went back, but Sefer went back and I did myself as well. But as far as I know, something may have continued. I'm not sure. It depends on the documents. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: No, that's okay. I -- I was really -- yes, well, thank you for those answers. I just wanted to clarify something with you: Is it within your knowledge whether or not the units -- the Sarajevo units, that being the 9th, the 10th, and the 2nd Independent Battalion, whether the elements of those units in Herzegovina went back to Sarajevo on or about the 20th? Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know nothing. I know nothing about the return of any of the units.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: That's okay. All right. Well, thank you for that. Apart from Sefer Halilovic returning to Sarajevo, to your knowledge did Suljevic, Bilajac, and Karic all also return to Sarajevo at around that time or possibly a day before?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. They were in the northern part. I didn't see them down there. I saw them in Sarajevo a few days later. We met. But I really don't know when.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. So the last time you saw -- just to be clear about that, you left them at the northern part of the front when you went down to Dreznica; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And you went back to Sarajevo yourself on what date?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We returned on the 19th in the evening, so on the 20th -- I think it was probably past midnight when we went through the tunnel to Sarajevo. We left on the 19th and probably in the early hours of the morning, just after midnight we got there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I understand. And can you just explain who you were with when you went back.

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We went back three times. I once returned with Cibo, and there was a bit of a crowd there. But then I went with Sefer from up there. I don't know whether then or before. It is possible, but Cibo was with us as well. I'm a bit confused. It is probably clear in the book, but I'm afraid I'm confused now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: No, that's okay. It's just -- it's just a detail. I was -- I won't pursue it with you. Very well. Thank you for that. Did you have the opportunity -- well, were you given the opportunity to look at the report drafted by the inspection team, that being Sefer, Suljevic, Karic and Bilajac, which they drafted on the 18th of -- of September? Were you shown that report at the time or not? I'm not suggesting you should have been, but I just need to ask whether you were.

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: At the time -- yes. Sorry. Just excuse me a moment now. Yes. Okay. Did you -- at that time, just in -- maybe the last two days or so of your time in -- in -- down at Dreznica and following the combat as you were down there, did anyone show you a cease-fire order at that time, an order signed by Stjepan Siber, as deputy for Rasim Delic?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody showed me any notice or information.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speaker please speak up -- the witness, I mean, because we can't hear him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Sorry I think it's the case that as I speak louder, the witness may speak --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Hodzic. Okay. Well, now I just -- just excuse me a moment while that's fixed. The interpreter has just asked if you wouldn't mind speaking slightly louder, please, Mr. Hodzic.

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. Now, the next thing I want to ask -- I want to ask you about now is moving forward to the time of Operation Trebevic and what happened on that occasion. Now, where were you actually when the news of Operation Trebevic first came to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 26th, in the morning, I was in my flat and I heard it in the morning on the radio, this alarming -- perhaps I shouldn't say "alarming," but this information, this notice coming from the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina that Caco and Celo were removed and the units -- and that it was being recommended to people not to even go out of their houses, not to go out into the street, and they didn't go to work on that day. And I think my newspaper called me at some point and asked me to go and ask for a statement from someone about what was going on, and I rang Sefer, and he was not willing to make a statement, and I didn't know what situation he was in, and I called Delic and I was told that he was out in the field. And then the newspaper at some point in the afternoon asked me once again to try and do something, to go to the 1st Corps. And late in the afternoon, early evening I went to the 1st Corps and basically it was like going to visit my friends, Karavelic and so on. But I was stopped at the gates, and I was being told, okay, just wait a minute. They will tell me something. At a certain point, a couple of policemen came along and they said, "Celo is surrendering. We must find some handcuffs for him." But they can't have any. They didn't have any handcuffs. So somebody brought a piece of string and they said, "Okay. We can tie his hands with this one." And Caco had not surrendered yet, and I was told -- the guard said, "Well, nobody wants to see you, you know. Can you please go away." And I was still not really aware of the fact that I was likely to run into problems as well. I did have problems two days later, but perhaps that's not of interest now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, no, frankly, it is of interest. But -- but up to this point, you -- you had -- you were simply doing your job as a journalist in attending at the 1st Corps, as you indicated. I see.

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, after that, you -- you were, however, in -- I use the word "invited" very loosely. But you were asked to attend at a police station. Can you just explain how that all came about and what took you to -- to be interviewed yourself.

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you know this story already. Munir Alibabic called me and I met with Sefer at the entrance, and I was asked to go in very quickly. And then the bit that you know, I met Sefer. And it was quite by chance. It was the State Security offices. And he said to me, "They want to blame me for what this gang did, for all these misdeeds, and then I'm saying, 'Okay. Yes. I created your state and your army and now you're free to arrest me.'" And then they called Mujezinovic who was the chief of the centre SDB. I can't remember the name of it. And I went up to him and he started shouting at me straightaway. And he was saying, "What is it that Sefer and you did once again? Take him away." And then I was taken to another room across the hall and there was an inspector standing by a table. And as soon as I went in, he said, "What you've got involved in is something that you would get at least 20 years in prison or even a death penalty for." And then I had a long conversation with him, 16 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. Well, now, I just want to take that all step by step. Firstly, you found yourself in -- at the downstairs part, and you saw Sefer Halilovic, and you spoke with him. And after that, Sefer was taken somewhere else. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He went for some other talks in the same building.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And did Sefer have a gun with him when -- when you saw him?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe so. I wasn't paying attention really. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you were then taken upstairs to meet somebody. And can you just explain, who is the person that you were taken upstairs to meet?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to what I found out later from some people, that inspector was Jasmin Sendijarevic, but it was Munir Alibabic, Enver Mujezinovic, and this Jasmin Sendijarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. Well, Munir Alibabic is the person who made the telephone call to you initially. Now it's moved to Enver Mujezinovic. Now, what did you understand Enver --

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: What did you understand his position to be, Enver Mujezinovic?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mujezinovic was the chief of the centre SDB, the State Security Service of the city of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: All right. Now, although I understand you're not -- not here as an expert witness in -- in the structures of the security organs, the SDB was an organ of the MUP, of the Ministry of the Interior; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Supposedly.
