utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: The Minister of the Interior at that time was an individual with the name Bakir Alispahic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. I knew him well as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, I understand. Now, Mujezinovic was a person about whom you had had discussions with Sefer while you were on the road in Herzegovina; is that true?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. And that was the first time that I saw him in my whole life.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, I understand. What did Sefer Halilovic tell you about his relations with Mujezinovic during the time when you were down in Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He mentioned Mujezinovic several times as a man who worked at this KOS. He said that he got there late and reported to the Armed Forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and his conclusion was that it was possible for him to go through Bijeljina and -- well, something along those lines. And for the most part, he was kind of against him. He -- he considered him an enemy, so to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Did Sefer indicate to you that in the past Mujezinovic -- Mr. Mujezinovic had attempted to damage Sefer's reputation by providing some documentation concerning Sefer's relations back in the old JNA days with the Secret Services there?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember that. I do not remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: That's okay. At all events, based on what Sefer told you, relations between Sefer Halilovic and Enver Mujezinovic were not friendly relations at all; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And I'm going to come to -- well, I'll deal with Mujezinovic now. You personally had had no dealings with Mr. Mujezinovic face to face before this day, as you've said. Just tell us about the first meeting that you had with him. What was the conversation that you had. Were any threats or nasty things said during that conversation?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I've already told you. But at any rate, so that was, apart from the fact that I had to go there, and he started shouting at me -- I mean, I've said it. I don't really know what you're getting at.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Sorry. Pardon me. I asked the question --

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I wrote about it. So he started threatening me, "What are you planning there?" Oh, yes, yes. There was something else. Okay. "Let's see who is going to slit whose stomach," or something. And I had no idea who was supposed to do anything like that. They said something -- "Well, we'll wait and see who slits whose stomach," apparently. And I had no idea what they were talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. Well, that's -- that was really the issue I was somewhat clumsily trying to get to, so thank you for trying to give the answer. But who made the comment about slitting bellies? Was that Mr. Mujezinovic?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mujezinovic was kind of threatening me. And then he didn't even wait for me to answer, and he just said, "Take him away."

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. And then you were taken away, and you then were interviewed by another individual, an inspector, for about 16 hours; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 16 hours. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. And in that time, were you given the chance to consult a lawyer or a family member?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No way. Of course not. I thought that I'd never get to see my children or my wife ever again. No lawyer, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And were there further threats made to you by this inspector which you've mentioned?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, one more time. I don't know at what stage of the conversation. Well, the way he talked to me was this. Okay? He was questioning me for two hours then and he was writing things down, and then after two hours he would start dictating. And then okay, he was dictating, and then he started writing things down or dictating things that I had heard for the first time. And I kind of argued with him. And quite energetically, more than once. And I said to him -- well, the way I assessed the situation at a certain point was that -- perhaps I was a bit slow off the mark, anyway. But I understood what game he was playing at rather late; that is to say, that whatever I said, whatever positive I had to say about Sefer, he was not going to write it down. And even if I made a neutral statement, he would turn it round and turn it into something horrible. And I said, "Well, what? Do you want to orchestrate a trial through me? Well, that's not something you can do. I am a religious man and I am afraid of God." And I know that I can be killed by Ustasha and Chetniks and the others, at the hands of all of them, but I don't want to die and have that sin on my soul." Then he relented slightly, but he had already mounted the whole operation. It was rather late. He had already written his report, and I really and truly believed -- well, I said to myself, I'm never signing this piece of paper. And some of the stuff -- I mean, when I looked at the text later -- were never mentioned in the course of the conversation and he wrote them down anyway. I don't know whether the whole thing was set up before, or maybe it wasn't. I mean, I don't even remember what exactly I heard. But there were two points specifically: First of all, apparently that Sefer Halilovic forbade me to write about those crimes, and there was another sentence to the effect that I was an eyewitness of both of the massacres. And then I spent a long time thinking about how -- how could I have signed those papers. First of all, I lost faith. I said to myself, Okay, the trial will go ahead and I'll be able to tell the truth. This is not important any more. And at one point he looked at me and he said, "Don't you know that we are at war and people get killed for this kind of thing?" And then later on -- I mean, at some point, this main person, then somebody who kind of sympathised with me a little bit more, when he the threatening guy left, he would say, "Okay. Forget about him. He's a fool. But you have to admit to something." And I thought, What should I admit to? And then I think it was a kind of a custody, because I think I was there in prison for about 26 hours. And I was convinced that -- Well, I said to myself, If I am sent to prison, it might be good. And even if I were sent to prison for 10 years, it wouldn't be so bad. And then that strict, rigid guy left. And I started reading through the text and I tried to correct a couple of things. And he said, "No, no, no, no, don't make any corrections. No way." And then the friendlier guy stayed behind and he said, "You know, what are you thinking of? You just sign these papers and my family is waiting for me and your family is waiting for you and then we can go home." And then I was surprised. I thought, How come? I'm going to be allowed to go home? But I should have read through all the pages and I had worked at the radio, but I knew that two minutes were enough to scan through a page. But I -- I signed every page, you know, within a minute. And when I finished, they said, "Okay. Great. Thank you very much. You can go home now." And I got home, and I didn't know what to do. Was I supposed to commit suicide or what? What was happening to me and so briefly --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: No mean to stop you -- to interrupt the account, it's just that there is a specific matter I have got to raise with you and this is an appropriate point to do it. At the time when you were with -- with these police, had you already heard of what happened to Caco, Musan Topalovic?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. It had already been announced that he had lost his life that, he had been killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. And was your understanding this: That Musan Topalovic handed himself in to the police and -- after a siege for a period of time, but then after that he was somehow killed? Is that what you heard?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard the same thing, that he had been killed, this way and that. But basically I heard he had been killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Incidentally, after he was killed, to your knowledge was Caco buried in the hero's cemetery?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not at first. And as far as I know -- I mean, there were a couple of possibilities. We are not sure. Initially at Zuc and then he was exhumed and taken somewhere else and then somewhere else again, but then I don't know exactly when. After the war, he did get a burial at -- at the most important cemetery in Bosnia and Herzegovina, the central cemetery for the fallen fighters at Kovaci. That's the main cemetery, basically.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. To your knowledge, on the 1st of -- well, you saw Sefer Halilovic going into the -- the hands of the -- of the police. When you saw Halilovic, did he appear to you to be in custody on that day when you yourself were questioned?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. It was broad daylight.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. And to your knowledge, from that moment on Sefer Halilovic played no role or no active role in the Army of Bosnia whatsoever; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't think this witness is in a position to answer what role Sefer played in the Bosnian army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, maybe this witness could give us a general account, because he's not in the army but he was a journalist.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, would you just remind giving an account such as the one His Honour just asked for then, just a general account as to what you knew, whether Sefer Halilovic played any further role, any active role, in the Army of Bosnia after that time you saw him in custody.

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a suspect in custody.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Or under house arrest, rather.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Did you know he was formally removed as Chief of Staff by an order on the 1st of November, 1993, an order of Alija Izetbegovic?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was announced soon after that Sefer had been removed and replaced as Chief of Staff by Enver Hadzihasanovic, Dzedo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. And after that time, to your knowledge, did Sefer Halilovic then form -- sometime later, many months or even years later, did Sefer Halilovic then form a political party?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He offered me to become the secretary-general of his party, but I refused.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. And what was the name of that party?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bosnian Patriotic Party.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. What was the name or is the name of the party of which Alija Izetbegovic and Bakir Alispahic were senior members?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Alija Izetbegovic was the president of the Party of Democratic Action. I don't know about Bakir Alispahic, whether he was a member of that same party or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. And at that time -- well, I withdraw that question. Just excuse me a moment, please. I'm sorry, Mr. Hodzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours. I have effectively finished the cross-examination now. I just -- there's one matter I'd just like to take instructions from Mr. Halilovic, if I might be permitted two minutes to do that. There's no need to adjourn the court. I'd be happy to just approach.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you. Just excuse me, Mr. Hodzic. We're nearly finished here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I'm grateful for the time. And I apologise for keeping the witness waiting there. It was a matter that I was just a little unsure about, and I've now had -- had it refreshed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: So that's the last thing I want to ask you about now before I finish the cross-examining is that during the time when -- when Sefer Halilovic was -- after he was finished his questioning and placed at home under house arrest, did you in fact go and visit him there, while he was under house arrest?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Many times. I spent a lot of time with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. And did he indicate to you that in his view the reason he'd been reduced to the status he now was essentially because of his political disagreement with Alija Izetbegovic? Over the different ways of dealing with Bosnia's future?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was very explicit about this. That was his own impression, that this had been the reason behind his removal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And finally, you're aware that in -- I'm not going to ask you about the details of the article, but you're aware that in 1995 in an article published in your newspaper, Oslobodjenje, Sefer Halilovic effectively called for a reopening of the investigation into the crimes at Grabovica in a very, very public way? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. When we talked about this, we were surprised that no one had raised the issue. There was the showdown with Caco and Celo earlier on, and yet no one seemed to be doing anything about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: That will be my final question for you: When you were asked questions by this inspector for 16 hours, did he show the least interest in finding the true killers at Grabovica?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you for your patience. Those are the questions I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Any redirect examination? Ms. Chana?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Your Honour, just very few questions and clarifications, if I may.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Mr. Hodzic, I'll not keep you very long. Now, you were asked by Defence counsel about Halilovic's correct way of behaving in the sense that he liked to work within a legal framework. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And in respect of that roadside meeting, one of the things Halilovic said was that Delic is taking away his powers and wants to leave him with purely administrative matters. From your own observations, Mr. Hodzic, when you were with him during this combat operations, was Halilovic performing administrative functions?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Sorry, I should interrupt that. It had better be clear whether this is being asked in an expert capacity or not. Because I don't object to some clarification, of course, in -- any that my friend sees fit. But it had better be made clear whether it's -- he's being asked whether these were technically administrative functions within the military hierarchy or whether it's just a general question as to his observations. If that's the case, I don't object to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Chana. Maybe you could clarify this question.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's -- it is a kind of a general question, in his own observation as to what exactly was his own perception of the duties that Halilovic carried out in the field.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Mr. Hodzic, you -- you -- my question was: While Halilovic was lamenting to you that his role has been reduced to purely administrative matters, what was your perception as you were shadowing him those days in Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you expect me to say? I'm not sure how I should explain this. This was no headquarters or staff, if you like. It was just a group of people down there. There was no administration to speak of. It was all in flux. I'm not sure how I should describe that. We were in flux, going hither and thither, all of us, the team members, and I was swept alongside with them. There was no real headquarters to speak of or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hodzic. Now, I'll -- I just want to take you back to the 9th, if I may. This is when Halilovic came and you whispered to him, "Have you heard about the -- the murders in Grabovica?" Did he ever say to you at the time, ^"I am now -- I have made arrangements for some sort of investigations," or "I've told Dzankovic to investigate this" at the time you were discussing it on the 9th of September?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, I was a very brief conversation. It took a minute or two at most. And the next day he told me, as we were on our way to Dobro Polje, that there were people around whose duty it was to investigate these matters. He didn't refer to Dzankovic specifically, but he said that there were people looking into that.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Mr. Hodzic, I just wanted to clarify the date Halilovic left -- left Herzegovina. And you had said that it was when -- I've got to --

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 19th.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: When you left, you parted company when you were in the northern part of the front in Dreznica. What date was that?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 14th, just when we returned from Dobro Polje and Prozor, the two of us reached Donja Jablanica. I asked to be driven further down to Dreznica because there was combat underway there. There was another man who was supposed to drive me there, but Celo turned up out of nowhere. He said, "You can come with us because my men are going there." I joined them on their way to Grabovica and Sefer stayed behind. So that was where we parted ways.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: So you really don't know what date Sefer Halilovic returned to Sarajevo, do you? Is it within your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean? I know. Of course I know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: What --

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 19th. The 19th of September, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Were you with him when he returned?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With him, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: All right. Now, thanks for that clarification. One last question, Mr. Hodzic: This is when learned counsel for the Defence was asking you about coordinating the operation and -- and those -- those questions. Do you remember those questions that were put to you, about Halilovic's role?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: You said you were shocked and surprised when he said that he was the coordinator. Could you please explain why you were shocked and surprised.

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first of all, it was the first time he told me that anyone was in charge of coordination at all. There was no coordinator there. Secondly, here was Sefer, a commander, symbolically speaking, turned coordinator of sorts. What was that supposed to mean? I wasn't aware of the order at the time. I wasn't aware of what was going on or what the substance of the order was. It was only much later when I saw the order appointing the inspection team to be led by Sefer Halilovic. Later when I investigated the Igman case that was a month later at least, I found another order by Delic dated the 3rd of August, 1993, which was very much like the other order but a bit -- it was issued a bit earlier on. Delic ordered a team to be set up and to be sent to Igman to help stabilise the situation over there, and so on and so forth. Zicro Suljevic was one member of the team; Rifat Bilajac and some other people too; and the team was to be led by Sefer Halilovic. I think that's what he was basing himself on when he wrote the next order. I see an analogy between the two orders. They looked the same to me. And if I had known about that order on the 19th of September, 1993, when I was trying to think of the questions and when I was thinking about how I should introduce him. Had I known about all of them, I would never have said that he was the commander of that operation. I looked through the files. You may have a document to that effect. I certainly don't, but no one ever called him commander, apart from me.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes. That will be my re-examination, Your Honour. Thank you very much, Mr. Hodzic, for your patience.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. At this stage, any documents to tender through this witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Ms. Chana?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Your Honour, I would like to tender all the documents that form part of this -- the exhibits that we -- the documents that we gave and it's got all the documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I see. Could you please read the numbers into the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It will be MFI161 -- Your Honour, this document, may I explain? It was supposed to have been admitted through Witness Gusic and it was a document I used in re-examination and somehow - I think it's been explained to Your Honours - it slipped the net and was not part of the exhibits that were admitted. So I would now tender that to be admitted. Then it's 288, Your Honour; 289; 290; 291; 292; and 281.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, there are a number of objections. I just wonder whether the witness needs to be detained any further. It's -- whether he needs to be concerned with this. And I just note the time. With the best will in the world, I don't think I can accomplish my answer in five minutes, Your Honours. I wonder whether it might be appropriate to release the witness. I'm happy to proceed this afternoon, and I can answer and deal with the matter without delay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I'm not Court's hands, frankly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, if we could finish this matter in 15 minutes, so we'd better not call our afternoon session, you know, because --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We'll have a recess, you know. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Try to -- well, you have already expressed your objections, you know --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: -- to those documents already. And so at this time, would you please be more concise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I just indicate this: What I'll do is -- I think I can accomplish what I have to do in ten minutes, and I just -- if -- if Your Honour wants the witness to stay, I'll -- I'll do it with the witness here. It just means speeches by me when the witness is here. My learned friend Mr. Weiner expressed a concern about that being done in the past. So I'm in the Court's hands. If you want me to start now, I'll start.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Ms. Chana, do you think we could release the witness at this stage?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I think the witness can be released, unless you think that tendering to have documents may somehow --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much indeed.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Witness, thank you very much indeed for coming to The Hague to give your evidence. Madam Usher will show you out of the room and we wish you a very pleasant journey back home. You may go now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you too, Your Honours. It has been an honour to be here and give testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Morrissey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Well, I just -- there -- I oppose the -- the tendering into evidence of the newspaper articles. I oppose the tendering into evidence of the book "The Unsealed Envelope," written by this witness. I oppose the tendering into evidence of the book by Halilovic. As to the diary, I have nothing to say about that now, in the circumstances. Your Honour, could I start with the issues of the articles and of the book, which now appear to be able to be dealt with as a group. In cross-examination, the witness was not cross-examined once about those documents at all. It's a matter for -- for the Court -- for the Tribunal to decide now, but you may form the view that the witness gave extremely detailed, live evidence on the relevant topics. Never did he say -- or never was there a topic upon which he needed to refresh his memory from the diaries. He did mention from time to time that there were some matters in there that he couldn't now recall, but they were all peripheral, small matters. I didn't press him about them and the learned Prosecutor didn't press him about them either. Now, when a witness gives good -- what I'd submit is good, responsive viva voce evidence, then that ought to be the evidence. The -- the materials -- the books and the articles have got real problems about them which have emerged from the evidence and I'm going to say what they are in just a moment. But in any event, even if they were perfect, they would be nothing ever than a previous statement by the witness. He's given effectively unchallenged -- unchallenged, uncontested evidence here in court and no one has -- well, I mean, that couldn't really be suggested, but no one has suggested any attack on his credibility or doubts about it. In fact the only time there was any what I might call clever cross-examination about that document and the dates about it, he had a very clear answer. He said, "Well, I may have made a mistake about the date." And he finished the controversy in one answer and did it very frankly and well. So that I'd submit his evidence doesn't need those other documents to be there and they are apt to distract. What I am afraid one might see is that at the end of the case, when the Sanction device is used to present closing argument, one will get pieces of the -- pieces of the articles, pieces of the book, whereas really what this Tribunal is about and what the public have seen and heard and what we've seen and heard is what we've said is there. And that's even if the book and articles are good. But the fact is they're not. They suffer from the following vices: First of all, they're done years after the event. The article is in 1999. The book subsequently. Secondly, they are not compiled from his memory. They are compiled from his memory plus other documents which he got from archival sources and from discussions that he had, no doubt in perfectly good faith, with various people. Possibly including the accused man, but also including Commander Delic, to whom he spoke, and other people to whom he spoke. Bilajac, and Suljevic have both been mentioned. We make no criticism of that. He's a good journalist and he's entitled to do exactly that. We don't criticise that. But books and the articles -- well, the book because they haven't tendered the other book. The book and the articles are imperfect. They're not his memory. They're a reconstruction by him, and he -- and -- and a legitimate reconstruction, but a reconstruction nevertheless. And because of that, they are not the best evidence. They're not the second-best evidence. They're -- they're quite remote. It would be different if they were used -- and that's why I said that the issue of how they're to be used in cross-examination is important. But Your Honours have seen -- I simply didn't cross-examine on those documents at all. The diary, I did. But that was probably tenderable in any event because it was quite contemporaneous and is there were good reasons why it should go. And anyway I don't oppose it. So that puts an end to that. So for those reasons I submit that there is no need whatsoever for that material to go in. There are some problems of detail about it. And if Your Honours are against me about admitting those materials, then certainly as far as the book is concerned, we've got some concerns about the selective nature of what has been chosen. Now, the Prosecutor in quite good faith, I have no doubt, has made selections of the material they want to put. But frankly, of the material --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Counsel please slow down for the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I have the warning to slow down, Your Honour. I feel the competing pressures, but I will be concise and slow. The material that's been sought to be tendered by the Prosecutor is a selection. Now, we don't suggest that it's in bad faith at all. Of course it's not, and my learned friend would not do any such thing. But it's a selection. And the original contains other material upon which -- which would give a fuller picture, if you like, of what this witness was saying in the book. But I didn't cross-examine him about the book. And frankly, it's just a distraction. When you -- when you turn now to see what Sefko Hodzic says, you've got a really good record, live in evidence, and it will be a distraction if if Prosecutor at the end of the case -- and I'm not suggesting they will, but I'll just dealing with the possibilities -- if they turn to say, "Well, we'd like you to look at what he said in an article in the year 1999." Now, that can't help. It can't have any weight. And it does serve to distract. When my friend said there's no prejudice, there is a prejudice to the Defence. The Defence doesn't want any strategies in this case. We want a clear presentation of the evidence. And there are many aspects of thiz evidence which it's quite obvious the Defence would rely on. We don't want to be turning to explain away pages in books from years intermediate between the time of the offences and today's trial. In particular, the book -- the passages that have been given to Your Honour from the book misses a number of sections, and I'll put them on the record now just so that there's no doubt about it. On pages 161 -- there's a part of page 165 missing, but that's -- 165 of the Bosnian version. We say that pages 178 to 197 are missing. 202 to 214 are missing. And 217 to 225 are missing. The titles of the chapters that appear not to have been provided are the chapter headed are: "Save Mostar in ten days," another chapter "Who shot at Haso Hakalovic," another chapter called "We are not an avenging army," has been left out. "We also cried together" is the fourth missing chapter. Chapter 5, "Why Caco was angry." Chapter 6, "The smell of living corpses." Sorry I'm giving -- it's not chapter 6 at all. It's the sixth one left out. These chapters are not numbered. "Croats like brothers to me" is another chapter. "The Boots of Marta Ibrahim" is another chapter. "A new trick on the Neretva" is another chapter. Now, frankly at least two of those chapters are concerned with later events. And I make it clear that we are not imputing ill faith to the Prosecutor, so my learned friend does not have to respond to any accusation like that and she would be entitled to be cross if we are making that. But what you're being given is a very partial selection. And that can't help you, so that there's all these different problems. That exist. The newspaper articles -- obviously, I made the comment and the Prosecutor in the past has said what they have to say about newspaper articles. As to Mr. Halilovic's book, he was present. There was a new development about that, quite frankly. I oppose its admission because -- for the reasons given before, it has to be acknowledged that it may stand in a different position than it did before because the Prosecutor did lead some new evidence about that. You'd be entitled to take that into account in the Prosecutor's favour in that it was proved that he was aware of the launch and -- and that he had a -- if you like, a more close knowledge than the previous witness. But, at the end of the day, I still oppose it being admitted through this witness because of the complaint I've made before about an investigator. That this should go through an investigator. He has no comment other than that he read it. Perhaps he can comment on it better than some others can, and he did comment on it. This is really a matter for the Tribunal, I have to say, but our position is that we oppose it. If I may put it in these terms: I strongly oppose the book and the articles, and those are the submissions I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. A very short response, Ms. Chana.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I would merely adopt the submissions I made to you earlier in this regard, Your Honour, but there was -- when Defence counsel points out the aspect of selective translation, and that's absolutely true, Your Honours, and we could as the Prosecution have it translated by CLSS and put it in at a later date, the entire book, if that -- that is -- that will solve the problem, Your Honour. We have only translated selective portions, and I -- I mentioned this to Your Honours earlier on. And the reason was that it was done at a late stage. It would have been very difficult, and I was also mindful of Your Honours' earlier decision that one should not burden the Court with -- with more paper than it needs. So they're not exactly missing, Your Honour, and that's important to know. The witness has been here. There was an opportunity to cross-examine him. And I would once again refer Your Honours to your own practice directions, that the rule is in favour of admissibility and the -- the criteria being -- the test being is relevant, it has probative value. Your Honours then is the question of weight to be given to it. No doubt Your Honours will look at the matters and give the appropriate weight. I think counsel has confuse the two concepts again: The admissibility and the weight to be given to the documents. And in his submissions, he is saying the -- the documents are not admissible. But essentially arguing the weight of the documents. So as I said, Your Honours, I will just merely adopt my earlier submissions on this, in view of the time, and they should be tendered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, after consultations with my colleagues, I would like to record the guidelines on the admission of the evidence issued by this Trial Chamber under Rule 89 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. At this point, the Trial Chamber would like to remind the parties of the basic distinction that exists between the admissibility of the documentary evidence and the weight the documentary evidence is given under the principle of free evaluation of the evidence. The mere admission of a document into evidence does not in itself signify that the statements contained herewithin will necessarily be deemed to be an accurate portrayal of the facts. The practice of this Tribunal is therefore in favour of admissibility, as the rule. As for those -- those documents publicly available, generally speaking they are admissible so long as they are relevant to this case and has a probative value in the contents. Of course there are some objections from the Defence team which I believe has been rightly recorded in the transcript and which will go to the weight of those evidence admitted at a later stage. This Trial Chamber has already stated that we would not like to see the whole book is translated into English and admitted into the evidence at this stage if there's no entire necessity for doing that. We only need the relevant part of that book to be admitted. At the same time, the Defence team also could have the opportunity to challenge the translation of that book or, if necessary, they also could introduce a certain part of the book into evidence in their case at a later stage. Therefore, the Bench makes the following ruling: That those documents tendered by the Prosecution are admitted into the evidence. It is so decided.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: As the Court pleases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, there's a couple of matters that have to be raised and they should be raised before Easter break, even though I acknowledge that we've raised a late stage. There's one I particularly have to raise because it affects the Prosecutor's scheduling. It's been indicated to me that next week the proposal is to call the witnesses Tirak, Okic, and Mujezinovic. Now, we're not ready for Mujezinovic. And we ask that the Prosecutor make other arrangements in relation to that. There are a number of reasons why we're not ready for him. Frankly, I'd prefer not to enunciate what they are right now. Broadly speaking, there are investigations that we wish to proceed with there. We don't do this out of any ill-faith with the Prosecutor. It's just the necessity that we have, unfortunately. I'm afraid to say the same thing really applies to the late-coming witnesses. It may be that the Prosecutor would have to consider turning to the Uzdol witnesses. I don't know what the answer so that is, and we'll attempt to -- to be cooperative. But we are not -- as currently advised, ready to deal with the witnesses Mujezinovic, Alispahic, and Delalic because we have further investigations that we have to perform. It's unfortunate. It's bad for the Prosecutors. We acknowledge it can cause inconvenience for them. And we apologise for that. But that is the reality of the situation we now find ourselves in. In relation to those people, we have a second point we have to make, and that is that in relation to all three, there really has to be some further Rule 68 material available, given what's now known on the public record about these persons and their current status. We ask that the Prosecutor look as earnestly as they possibly can in the next few days to see what Rule 68 material they may chance to have. In a case where inquiry notice is at issue, the Prosecution are very much on notice as to the situation relating to those three individuals and they really have got to tell us what they have and -- and so we asked that that be done as soon as it can be. Your Honours, I'd just finally -- I'm sorry. And there are many matters that we could raise here and I had thought they were going to the evening session. Your Honours -- yes, those are the matters. There is one other matter. There's a document we have to tender into the evidence, and that is MFI293, the single page of the diary which I forgot to -- to offer. But those other two matters are important. A final matter is this: Although we haven't done so yet, the witness Okic, who's coming next week, is the bearer of a -- a potential exhibit. The Prosecutors wish to elicit into evidence through Mr. Okic a statement said to be made by Halilovic at the time he was interviewed at around the same time that this witness was interviewed by the -- the Trebevic investigators. We oppose the admissibility of that interview. It's not fair to spring that at the last minute on -- on either Mr. Okic, who would then sit is there while a legal argument took place, or the Tribunal, who would then be forced to deal with some relatively significant legal issues at the time. Therefore we have decided that we will file a motion and we thought we'd -- in a rush we'd file it before Easter. We don't expect the Prosecutor to reply to us until -- as soon as they can. But we know it will be later. We thought that we'd better rush to do that now rather than cause a controversy next week. So we are going to file that. We mention that to indicate that we don't think that should be admitted into evidence. The final matter that I was going to raise concerns the deposition of Mr. Karic. That issue has got to be faced. Mr. Re raised it. Your Honour raised it with Mr. Re. He said he'd come back. We think that should be played to the Court and Mr. Re or the Prosecution should respond to that sometime soon. Those are the matters, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Weiner, very, very briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, just very briefly. For next week we cannot change the schedule or bring another witness instead of Mr. Mujezinovic in on Friday. That's number one. So if we are going only going to be running with two witness next week and since they are going to be filing late -- a last-motion, I'd request that we not sit on Wednesday. That we get a chance to see what this motion is, have a chance to talk to the witness, who will only be arriving on Monday. So we won't even see him until Tuesday. We're going to have to spring a motion on the witness on Tuesday. If we're not going to be bringing Mr. Mujezinovic -- and any witnesses for the following week were those other individuals that were mentioned -- I'd have to see and also deal with the Victim and Witness Unit if we can start making schedule changes. This -- we have taken these witnesses. We've moved them towards the end of our case, which is in April. We have them. We want to get them here, have them testify. And I see no reason why they can't testify. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, thank you very much. I believe that this Trial Chamber has made a decision concerning of the further investigations of certain witnesses. I will not go into the details about that decision because it is filed ex parte and confidential. But anyway, we believe that the Defence request for postponement of the testimony of Mujezinovic is reasonable. So the request from the Defence is granted. At the same time, I believe that the Prosecution has the consistent obligations to disclose any documents concerning of Rule 68, if there's any.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: If there is any.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And we have continued to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Of course. But I just want to remind you of this on obligation. And as for the document tendered by the Defence, I see no objections from the Prosecution team. That's the translation of the diary.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Not at all, Your Honour. And in respect of that, may I also say that while the whole diary is in ringtail, as it were, we only want our last two pages as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Again, not to burden the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I understand that. So the document is admitted into the evidence. I believe that's all I have to say at this stage. And I would like to thank the interpreters, the typewriters, and all the technicians for their a-little-bit-longer working hours this morning, but anyway, we don't have to sit this afternoon. So I wish everybody a good Easter, and the hearing is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 30th day of March, 2005, at 2.15 p.m.
